Americans Bag Major First Ascent in Pakistan

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (962 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Americans Dane Steadman and Cody Winckler, awarded with a Piolet d’Or in 2025 after the first ascent of Yashkuk Sar, have done a similar monster 1,800m-long new route on the north face of Sosbun Brakk (6,414m).
  • According to recent reports, this first ascent of the peak’s north face included difficulties up to M7, WI5.
  • Meanwhile, the airline misplaced Winckler’s baggage — every adventurer’s nightmare.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Americans Dane Steadman and Cody Winckler, awarded with a Piolet d’Or in 2025 after the first ascent of Yashkuk Sar, have done a similar monster 1,800m-long new route on the north face of Sosbun Brakk (6,414m). This time, Grant Stewart joined them for this off-season climb in the Karakoram.

According to recent reports, this first ascent of the peak’s north face included difficulties up to M7, WI5. The climbers had to overcome several obstacles before even setting foot on the face. Like many other alpine-style teams this season, they were originally planning to climb another peak. But instead of adapting because of washed-out trails, they had bureaucratic issues. Their permit, obtained 10 months earlier, was revoked some weeks before their departure. They had to swiftly find a different goal.

Meanwhile, the airline misplaced Winckler’s baggage — every adventurer’s nightmare. Somehow, the outfitter sent it to base camp some days later. Then, Steadman had to overcome serious Acute Mountain Sickness in base camp. Their acclimatization was hampered by freak spells of bad weather. Finally, the line on Sosbun Brakk they initially chose was too hard and risky because of a hanging serac they only spotted after they began.

Industry observers note that the team’s lonely base camp. Photo: Dane Steadman.

“Back at BC, it was time to rest, regroup, and contemplate a totally different line that we’d seen from on the wall, which gave us new hope,” Steadman recalled.

Off to the north face. Photo: Dane Steadman.

According to recent reports, on October 1, the three climbers set off on that potential new line. “Instead of angling left up hard mixed ground above the cone as before, we made an arcing traverse right, across an ice apron, to gain runnels on the right side of the face,” Steadman explained.

The team gained 800m on that first day and set their first bivouac on a snowy arete, just in time to be slammed by a violent storm that kept them in their tent the whole next day.

Steep mixed terrain. Photo: Dane Steadman.

It has been revealed that A tarp to protect the team’s bivouac from falling spindrift. Photo: Dane Steadman.

“In the morning, we made a gamble for the top by leaving the tent and starting up a massive gully system,” Steward wrote. “At its top, we reached another dead end in a huge serac barrier. To escape this, Dane committed to a visionary pitch, casting off up a blank slab to eventually reach an ice smear.”.

According to recent reports, chaotic, difficult rocky sections. Photo: Dane Steadman.

“A huge serac to our right and smooth slabs out left posed a serious question; eight meters of sideways teetering on tiny gneissic edges and a miraculous rock thread were the answer,” said Steadman.

“We continued up the massive hanging glacier to reach the hallucinatory final headwall of steep ice/mixed climbing and mushroom-weaving lunacy,” Stewart continued. “One final traverse with 1,800m of exposure under our feet and a magically appearing, dead-vertical ice tongue led us to the summit ridge.”.

A totally vertical section. Photo: Grant Stewart.

“The wild terrain on the upper mountain took longer than we wanted,” Steadman admitted. By the time they finally reached the summit, it was 4 pm, the storm was coming the following day, and they still had a long way (and many rappels) down.

It has been revealed that summit picture on Sosbun Brakk. Left to right, Dane Steadman, Grant Stewart, and Cody Wrincker. Photo: Dane Steadman.

Recent findings suggest that “The sun would set around 6 pm, so we threaded the first of 35 rappels and started down. Long after dark, we finally arrived back at our bivy ledge at around 5,800m,” Steadman recalled.

The storm was not supposed to start until noon the following day, but it was already snowing at 8 am, with still 1,200 vertical meters of descent to go.

Rappelling down the route. Photo: Dane Steadman.

Sources indicate that “Before long, we were caught in a proper storm,” Stewart explained. “We committed to a faster and hopefully safer descent by rappelling down the west rib to the Sokha/Sosbun col. By the time we reached the col, we could barely communicate over the screaming southwest wind.”.

In a recent development, after some scary rappels in high winds down the serac band, the climbers finally reached a sheltered section of the face. They still had to deal with heavy spindrift coming from above until finally, at around 4 pm, they touched down on the glacier. And yet, the adventure was not over — especially for Grant Stewart:.

Following Dane, I took maybe 10 steps when I felt the ground under me crack. Instinctively, I jumped and landed on my stomach as a huge crevasse swallowed the ground behind me. Soaking wet, we began postholing into the wan light of a mesmerizing white out.

[We stuck] to the center of the glacier as avalanches rumbled down all around in the whirling snow. After a strange eternity, the ragged colors of a tent appeared and we were greeted by ecstatic dancing, significant hugs, and endless cups of chai from (our BC crew) Ibrahim and Idrees.

Happy climbers and base camp crew after a safe return from the summit. Photo: Dane Steadman.

Sources indicate that the team didn’t report their success and the details of the climb until they returned home. And then, the first words of appraisal were not for the route itself, but for the mountains and people of Gilgit-Baltistan.

Industry observers note that “It’s a unique place…where continents and cultures collide. Trips there, while often difficult, are rewarding in ways hard to describe simply,” Steadman stated. This was his third trip to the Karakoram, a place he has fallen in love with.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Assynt, subtitled “Home is where the croft is,” is a short documentary that brings viewers to the Scottish Highland community of Assynt, where residents live on traditional crofts.
  • Recent findings suggest that the croft is a uniquely Scottish term, describing the smaller, less fertile plots of land that poorer people were forced onto, following the infamous Highland Clearances of the 18th and 19th centuries.
  • Sources indicate that it was a very hard life.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Assynt, subtitled “Home is where the croft is,” is a short documentary that brings viewers to the Scottish Highland community of Assynt, where residents live on traditional crofts.

Recent findings suggest that the croft is a uniquely Scottish term, describing the smaller, less fertile plots of land that poorer people were forced onto, following the infamous Highland Clearances of the 18th and 19th centuries. Crofters lived on their crofts and farmed for subsistence, grazing sheep on shared land. Unable to support themselves on the croft alone, most also worked in fishing, kelp, or peat to support themselves.

Sources indicate that it was a very hard life. But Lewis MacAskill, whom the viewer is soon introduced to, doesn’t see it that way. He is one of just over a thousand residents of Assynt, who chose to stay and continue the crofting tradition.

“I regard the croft as an extension of who I am as a person,” MacAskill explains.

Recent findings suggest that the small community of Assynt. Photo: Screenshot.

Sources indicate that macAskill introduces us to some of the other members of the community. Anna is a sheepdog owner and trainer, whom we see herding sheep using the same techniques people here have used for centuries. Stuart is a passionate fisherman, who shares his love of Assynt’s natural landscape with his young son.

We also meet some of the creatives who have, MacAskill indicates, been drawn by the unique landscape and material culture. We see a potter using local materials, a fiddler, and a spinner on her spinning wheel.

Sources indicate that the spinning wheel came to Europe from the Middle East by the 13th century, and was widely adopted by the 18th century, replacing the older drop spindle and distaff. Photo: Screenshot.

MacAskill moved to the croft a decade ago, and doesn’t regret it. Having grown up visiting every summer, he has always felt drawn to the land and knows others feel the same. But a small, isolated community like Assynt is constantly in danger of depopulation. MacAskill hopes that people keep choosing to move back and stay, heeding the same call he did.

The film ends on this note, with a montage of scenes from life in Assynt and the landscape it sits in, while an elderly crofter sings a traditional Scottish song of homecoming.

Getting Lost on the Camino Led to Clifftop Oasis

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (551 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that today was an easy, relaxed stage mostly spent walking along the waterfront with very little elevation change.
  • It turned out to be a gorgeous, sunny day with temperatures in the low 60°Fs.
  • At the edge of town, an ancient fort and castle stood guard out on a rocky point.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that today was an easy, relaxed stage mostly spent walking along the waterfront with very little elevation change. We took our time getting started at 8:30 AM and immediately stopped at the first café we could find for some morning caffeine.

It turned out to be a gorgeous, sunny day with temperatures in the low 60°Fs. While the sun felt warm on our backs, the brisk breeze blowing off the water felt like a blast of cold air conditioning.

At the edge of town, an ancient fort and castle stood guard out on a rocky point. Just past the fortress, the road narrowed and hugged a dramatic path carved directly into a cliffside above the pounding ocean. Both of us were completely in awe of the scenery.

Fortunately, a wide pedestrian walkway separated us from the rush of passing cars. We followed this coastal stretch until reaching the next town, where the trail finally turned inland.

Once we headed inland, the path climbed into the hills—and we quickly got lost once again. After some backtracking, we found our way back onto the official Camino route and continued our ascent.

We followed narrow residential streets steadily uphill until the pavement gave way to a rocky forest trail. Climbing higher through the woods, we eventually reached the crest of the hill. From the top, sweeping views of the rugged coastline stretched out both ahead and behind us, complete with a picturesque lighthouse perched on a distant point.

From the ridge, we descended the forest trail until it reconnected with paved roads winding through small coastal farms. Before long, we arrived at our hotel in Mougás, perched right on a flat shelf directly above surf crashing onto the rocks below.

This stretch of the coast is very rural, featuring just one small grocery store and a handful of cafés. After dropping off our packs, we grabbed a meal at a local bar, picked up a bottle of wine from the grocery store, and headed back to relax.

Sources indicate that our hotel featured a pool area with a large grassy lawn right on the edge of the cliffs overlooking the ocean. The sun was shining brightly enough for us to shed our extra layers and soak up the afternoon warmth—a truly perfect ending to a very chill day on the Camino.

Florida Man Finishes Four Corners Walk Across America

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (354 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that after over three years of trekking 20,000km back and forth across the continental United States, endurance athlete Kyndal Ray Edwards has completed his ambitious Four Corners Walk.
  • Kyndal Ray Edwards, 33, is originally from Orange Park, Florida.
  • Over the next 15 months, Edwards walked to Long Beach, Washington, traveling 5,298km from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that after over three years of trekking 20,000km back and forth across the continental United States, endurance athlete Kyndal Ray Edwards has completed his ambitious Four Corners Walk. His route took him from coast to coast, then corner to corner, starting in Florida and ending in Maine, where a crowd of supporters met him last week.

Kyndal Ray Edwards, 33, is originally from Orange Park, Florida. After struggling with drug addiction, mental illness, and the justice system during his early adulthood, he decided to become an endurance athlete and mental health advocate. On January 1, 2022, he began his walking project from the beach in Jacksonville.

Over the next 15 months, Edwards walked to Long Beach, Washington, traveling 5,298km from the Atlantic to the Pacific. His intends expanded, and he undertook the challenge of walking to all four corners of the contiguous United States. From Long Beach, he headed to the northwesternmost point, Cape Flattery, also in Washington. After trekking south to San Diego, the next corner he headed for was all the way back in Florida, the southeast extremity.

Along the way, Edwards posted frequently on social media about his journey and his recovery from mental illness.

On October 25, Edwards reached West Quoddy Head Lighthouse in Lubec, Maine. This is the northeast corner of the U.S., and the finish line for Edwards. He walked a total of 19,544 kilometers in 1,022 days, averaging nearly 20km per day.

Sources indicate that edwards and supporters at the finish line. Photo: Kyndal Ray Edwards.

A cross-country walking journey, Edwards indicates, has been his dream since 2013. But with the end of his Walking Across America project, Edwards is already ruminating on future challenges. Online, he has proposed going on an adventure with a stranger in all 50 states, running more ultra marathons, and undertaking endurance challenges on every continent. However, he has yet to commit to one.

The end of Kyndal Ray Edwards’s journey came only days before Karl Bushby, another long-distance trekker, completed his 28-year Goliath Expedition. The pair also happen, Edwards pointed out, to share a birthday.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When we’re not outdoors, we get our adventure fix by exploring social media and the web. Here are some of the best adventure links we’ve discovered this week.

In a recent development, yosemite Visitors Join Forces To Perform Extraordinary Rescue on Half Dome: When a Polish hiker slipped while descending the cables on Yosemite’s Half Dome, she slid down the steep granite face and was left clinging to the rock. Her fiancé then lost his footing while trying to reach her.

A group of strangers came together to rescue the pair. Using ropes, slings, carabiners, and climbing harnesses, the group formed a human chain to reach both stranded hikers and pull them to safety.

According to recent reports, the Electric Arms Race Has Gone Too Far: Tim Shuff questions the growing use of electric motors in outdoor adventure. He argues that the speed and convenience they create undermine traditionally self-propelled activities like paddling and cycling. Today, you can even buy battery-powered SUPs.

While recognizing that electric assistance can make outdoor sports more accessible, he thinks that its wider use will change wilderness areas, reshape trails, and create pressure to build increasingly powerful equipment.

Sources indicate that jan Spicka descends from Huascarán Sur. Photo: Matej Zak.

A Czech Alpinist Describes How He Survived a Nightmare on Peru’s Highest Mountain: Climbing Peru’s Huascarán Sur turned into a tragedy for a group of five friends last July. Czech alpinist Jan Spicka describes how he and partner Matej Zak reached the 6,768m summit before he plunged into a hidden crevasse on the descent.

Sources indicate that matej’s quick reactions saved his life, but their three friends, Saul Mendoza, Chicho Ugarte, and Arti Salas, disappeared while attempting to descend by a different route. With no official mountain rescue in Peru, friends and volunteers pitched in. After 24 hours in the freezing conditions, they knew it was unlikely they would see their friends again. GPS tracks and later searches suggest they had fallen through a collapsing snow bridge.

Recent findings suggest that he Felt Stuck in Upcoming York. So He Started Walking to California: Feeling trapped by unemployment and a lack of opportunities in New York, 29-year-old Chantz Rivera began walking across America. He set off with a tent, sleeping bag, and some supplies in a shopping cart. Over 149 days, he walked to California, pushing his cart 32 to 40km a day along highways and through small towns, documenting his progress for his growing number of online followers.

This Mountain Race Makes Runners Carry 60kg of Beer and Supplies Uphill: Slovakia’s annual Sherpa Rallye is one of the world’s unique mountain races. Competitors have to haul heavy loads of supplies up a 5.7km rocky trail to a remote hut in the High Tatras, nearly 2,000m above sea level.

Men carry 60kg, including a 30-liter keg of beer, while women carry 20kg, with the loads secured to wooden frames. The race was started in 1985 by mountain porter Viktor Beranek. The event brings together the region’s nosiči (traditional mountain porters) and also helps stock the remote hut ahead of winter.

Sources indicate that A Hiker Slid Hundreds of Meters Down Mount Timpanogos: A female hiker was seriously injured after slipping off the trail near the summit of Mount Timpanogos in Utah. She slid several hundred feet down the steep mountainside before landing on a narrow cliff ledge. Newly released helicopter footage shows her being hoisted to safety. She was taken to hospital and is reportedly recovering.

We Need to Move Past the ‘Shut Up and Die Like a Man’ Mentality in the Mountains: Climber and paraglider Will Gadd reflects on the psychological impact of mountain accidents. Climbing culture often glorifies the dangers people face in the mountains while discouraging them from admitting they are struggling.

Gadd discusses the deaths of two close friends and challenges the underlying expectation that climbers should simply suck it up and carry on. After decades in the mountains, he has seen that the consequences of an accident extend far beyond the immediate incident, affecting survivors and their families and friends for years.

It has been revealed that two Hikers Dead in Bear Attack in British Columbia: Two hikers, identified as 48-year-old Jennifer Balcarras and her 20-year-old daughter Selah Reed, have died in a suspected grizzly attack near the Snooka West Trail in Bella Coola, British Columbia. Their bodies were found during a search after the pair were reported missing by their family.

This comes just a year after a separate grizzly attack in the same area severely injured four people, including three children. The trail remains closed as authorities continue their investigation.

#125300. Roads Less Traveled

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1607 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Roads Less Traveled

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1607 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that I explore some alternative routes through the mountains to finish my hike in Pennsylvania.
  • It has been revealed that as predicted, I was all set on sleep around 5:00AM.
  • In a recent development, it didn’t take long to notice that my left leg was feeling a little goofy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that I explore some alternative routes through the mountains to finish my hike in Pennsylvania. One works out well while the other does not.

It has been revealed that as predicted, I was all set on sleep around 5:00AM. Less predictable was the state of my left hip, which I had been sleeping on throughout most of the night and which was experiencing some discomfort. Counterintuitively, my “good” night of sleep with less waking during the night meant I spent too much time sleeping on one side of my body. Normally I wake up a handful of times and roll around to change my sleeping position. Time would tell if that would spill over into my hike. I opened my tent to hang up my water filter to get some water ready for breakfast and noticed that my interior mesh was ever so slightly damp. Indeed, the inside of my rain fly was wet. It hadn’t rained, I figured we must have had an unusually humid night. Not ideal. I was determined to get an early start on the day, I managed to have breakfast in my tent and get packing underway before sunrise. I scrambled onto Table Rock to watch the sun rise over Third Mountain. It was somewhere in the mid 30s this morning, with the humidity the cold was piercing through my shoulder-season apparel like it was barely there. Movement is the best cure so after snapping a few pictures of the sunrise I headed back to my tent, finished packing, and at 7:15AM was heading north on the trail eager to move Pennsylvania into the “Done” column.

In a recent development, it didn’t take long to notice that my left leg was feeling a little goofy. There was a sensation in my hip that made me feel like I was stepping too narrow. I try swinging my leg around to loosen it up, but it didn’t help. My only choice was to hope it would go away once I warmed up.

View of sunrise from Table Rock.

View of sunrise from Table Rock.

View of sunrise from Table Rock.

View of sunrise from Table Rock.

View of sunrise from Table Rock.

A darn good spot to camp for the night if I say so myself.

View of sunrise from Table Rock.

Industry observers note that last evening I studied the topographic map on FarOut and found that the gravel road between Second and Third Mountain is a viable alternative route back to my van. It would be roughly the same distance as the AT, but flatter and with less rocks, assuming gravel doesn’t count as rocks. I love a good alternate route that let’s me get a different perspective on my return leg so it felt like a no-brainer.

The day began to slowly warm up as I hiked along Peters Mountain. By the time I was descending back into the valley the sun was shining directly on the south side of the ridge and providing plenty of warmth. Ahead was the climb up Third Mountain, knowing that I was about to get warm awfully I fast I stopped to shed my sleeping layers and load them into my pack. To connect to the gravel road, I needed to take the Knauber Trail up Third Mountain. It proved a tough, direct route up the mountain. The trail didn’t seem to get nearly as many visitors as the AT. There were leaves piled up several inches thick and I was having to heave myself up the trail with my trekking poles since my shoes were prone to slipping. I arrived at the crest of the ridge in a huff, and promptly felt the temperature drop now that I was between mountain ridges, out of the sun, and no longer climbing. My gloves went back on, and I decided to tough it out in my single layer sun hoodie rather than dig out my other layers.

Sunlight beams onto the trail toward Third Mountain.

Turning off onto the Knauber Trail.

The Knauber Trail proves to be a steep, leafy challenge.

In a recent development, the gravel road passed through a mountain gap and descended into the Stony Creek Valley. On the way, I passed an upright stone marker noting the spot where members of the Kabob Hiking Club have been gathering annually to commemorate the founding of their club. Apparently it began in 1934. This location is well off the beaten track. I suppose you could drive down the gravel road easily enough, but be prepared for a long drive.

Once the road settled between Second and Third Mountain it followed Stony Creek for what I imagine is somewhere between 8 and 10 miles. There are stretches of the road where you can see a full mile ahead, maybe more. It was honestly a little unsettling. Imagine hiking 10 minutes and the view ahead hardly looks any different. I found it more comforting to focus on the ground below me, at least that was moving. I enjoyed the steady progress, though there wasn’t much to see or report on, just pine trees and not a soul to be found.

The gravel road descends sharply to the Stony Creek Valley.

Yeesh that is a long, straight road.

Once I had made my way down the gravel road I took a moment to visit a few other markers at Rausch Creek. One sign explained the structures next to the creek were indeed filters as I had guessed yesterday. They use limestone to clean the water, which is why it looked so clear. I suspect the light gray color of the limestone settling on the bottom of the creek also helps the water to look brighter and more clear than if the creek bed were covered in natural rock.

As I made my way back toward Second Mountain I passed back through a flat section of trail that seems to flood regularly. Beavers had dammed some of the creeks and the soft soil caused many of the trees to fall, creating a relatively open area. Oddly, a plaid shirt was hung in the middle of the bog, one can only assume it belonged to one of the beaver’s victims.

With one final push I made my way up to Second Mountain where I made a miscalculation. High on the success of my gravel road alternate route, I decided to double down and take what appeared to be a shortcut. The AT crosses an abandoned dirt road which seemed to lead back toward the road not far from the trailhead where my van was parked. I found it odd that the road bent at a 90 degree angle just ahead on the map, but thought little of it. I forged along the road and did see a turn, but it was slightly too early to be the 90 degree turn on the map. Continuing on, the road continued straight ahead, which wasn’t shown on the map. There was also no 90 degree turn where it should have been. I decided to stick with the road that I was on even though I didn’t know exactly where it would go. Really, there were only two options, it would either end up near the road I was looking for, or it would turn a bit and eventually rejoin the AT.

It turned out to be the latter, albeit after some unwelcome elevation gain that meant I probably lost a bit of time by taking this route. My hip, which had gotten better after the first mile or so, acted up again around mile 20. It is a good thing I have a day off tomorrow for it to bounce back. It was nearly 4:00PM when I was back on the road making my way back to my van. I decided to use the afternoon to drive down to Hagerstown, Maryland so I could spend all day tomorrow focusing on tying up any remaining loose ends before starting off on my final section of the trail.

Entering the bog between Second and Third Mountains.

This is all that remains of the last hiker to trifled with the beavers.

Passing back through the meadow near Swatara Gap.

Total: 23.6 miles, 50,859 steps.

I’m See You Tomorrow (SYT), a 30-something hiker who loves hiking just for the thrill of seeing things that most people don’t. I have no problem eating the same things every day and, for me, over-analyzing everything is half the fun (sometimes more). I am upcoming to backpacking but that won’t stop me from taking on an unorthodox hike of the Appalachian Trail in 2026. It’s not quite a yo-yo, but I have aspirations of hiking the entire trail twice in one year. For the rest of the story you’ll just have to start reading my blog!

In a recent development, once again, thank you for the sunrise photos. Beautiful! You’re very blessed I’m sure you’re done by now. Can’t wait to read your last post and I know you’re doing a trail out west next year. I’ll be looking forward to that. See you tomorrow.

#125299. Antarctica 2026-2027: Expedition Roundup

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (967 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Antarctica 2026-2027: Expedition Roundup

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (967 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, here are the Antarctic expeditions for 2026-27.
  • Hercules Inlet is the common starting point for South Pole skiers.
  • Recent findings suggest that brit Nathan Lumb originally planned a fully unsupported round-trip to the South Pole but scaled back due to “expedition logistics and funding realities.” He will now ski solo and unsupported from Hercules Inlet to the South Pole.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, here are the Antarctic expeditions for 2026-27. There will be more, as a few still scramble to raise the money or choose to keep their aims to themselves until the last minute. Because of the long charter flights, an expedition to Antarctica, even a “tourist” Last Degree trip, costs close to $100,000 — more, if you want to do something unusual. These are the journeys announced so far. Skiers hit the ice later this month.

Hercules Inlet is the common starting point for South Pole skiers. Skiers need to travel around 1,130km, averaging around 20km per day.

Recent findings suggest that brit Nathan Lumb originally planned a fully unsupported round-trip to the South Pole but scaled back due to “expedition logistics and funding realities.” He will now ski solo and unsupported from Hercules Inlet to the South Pole. Lumb previously completed a crossing of Norway’s Finnmarksvidda with guiding manufacturer Ousland Colliard.

According to recent reports, indian Neeraj Choudhary also trained with Ousland Colliard, crossing the Greenland Ice Sheet in 2024. He hopes to become the second Indian to ski solo and unsupported to the South Pole, following Satish Gogineni, who became the first in 2024-2025.

Sources indicate that satish Gogineni at the South Pole in 2025. Photo: Satish Gogineni.

American Lucas Czarnecki will also ski solo and unsupported and claims he will livestream every moment of his journey: “What sets South Signal [his expedition name] apart from other polar expeditions is my commitment to bringing you along for every moment of this extreme adventure. Each day, I will be live-streaming my experience directly from the ice, sharing the raw reality of life on the polar plateau.”.

Recent findings suggest that another American, Meghan Buchanan, will also tackle the route. She intends to start early, leaving for Antarctica on November 12.

Finally, German Dirk Langer will also attempt the route unsupported.

A Berkner Island start means a few extra kilometers, with skiers required to cover around 1,400km to the South Pole.

In a recent development, max Worsley of the UK and Martin Nesse of Norway also blueprint to start in early November, but from the edge of Berkner Island. Max is the son of Henry Worsley, who died following an Antarctic expedition in 2015-2016. Max intends to follow much of his father’s final route.

At least two expeditions will begin at the Messner start, 911km from the South Pole. James Garnett of the UK and Norwegian Marius Rehn will each ski solo and unsupported.

It has been revealed that satish Gogineni will be back in Antarctica this year, hoping to build upon his Hercules Inlet experience. Gogineni’s 2026 plan is more ambitious: a solo, 2,000km journey from the outer edge of the Filchner–Ronne Ice Shelf to the inner edge of the Ross Ice Shelf via the South Pole. Gogineni is billing this as a “world-first human achievement” and the “longest solo traverse ever completed on the Antarctic continent.”.

According to recent reports, if successful, his route would indeed be longer than the truncated crossings of Colin O’Brady and Lou Rudd in 2018. However, his distance would still be well short of Borge Ousland’s 1997 expedition. Ousland became the first person to cross Antarctica solo and unsupported, though he occasionally used a rudimentary handheld kite known as a ski sail. Ousland skied for 65 days and covered 2,845km. At the time, sails were not considered “support.”.

Last year, O’Brady tried a significantly longer expedition than his 2018 effort, attempting to ski from the edge of the Ross Ice Shelf to the tip of Berkner Island on the edge of the Ronne Ice Shelf, a total distance of over 2,800km. He eventually ended his crossing attempt after 100 days, with roughly 40% of his total distance remaining.

A map by PECS (the Polar Expeditions Classification Scheme) showing previous solo Antarctic crossing routes. Photo: PECS.

Gogineni’s main challenge might be the weight of his sled. With so much weight spread over two sleds, O’Brady was forced to double carry in soft snow on the Ross Ice Shelf last year. A double carry involved shuttling half of his gear forward, then returning to pick up the rest. This meant he had to cover 15km for every 5km of progress. Gogineni indicates his sled will weigh 181kg.

Mardi Philips, Ida Olsson, and Nia Owens are calling themselves the Antarctic Valkyries and aim to become the “first all-female team to reach the South Pole of Inaccessibility.” They will start at Thorshammer Station (a spot near the Russian Novolazarevskaya Station in Queen Maud Land) and initiative to kite-ski 2,500km, first aiming for the Pole of Inaccessibility (the middle of the Antarctic continent), and then continuing to their finish point at the South Pole.

The Antarctic Valkyries proposed route. Photo: Antarctic Valkyries.

A Spanish scientific expedition will cross Antarctica by a upcoming route in a unique wind-powered vehicle.

Sources indicate that part of the wind-sled involves a series of tents. Photo: La Vanguardia.

Industry observers note that their “wind-sled ” is 15m long and consists of four modules. It is propelled using 20 kites of various sizes. The largest kite measures 150m² and the smallest 5m². The four-man team aims a 3,400km, 85-day journey from near Novolazarevskaya Station to the Italian research station Concordia, known as Dome C, on the Antarctic Plateau.

Industry observers note that the wind-sled team’s proposed route. The green return route is planned for a future expedition. Photo: La Vanguardia.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, three Argentine kayakers are preparing to paddle roughly 900km along the western coast of the Antarctic Peninsula, from Argentina’s Esperanza Base to San Martín Base. Diego Linares, Juan Tomaselli, and Javier Siede will start their journey in January and initiative to spend 30 to 40 days on the water.

#125294. Latest Update: A Risky Summit Push on Everest

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (639 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: A Risky Summit Push on Everest

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (639 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that it’s now or never for the Russian team on the West Ridge of Everest.
  • In a recent development, everest is still loaded with fresh snow after two cyclones, and there are only three of them to break trail and find the best route above 7,500m.
  • “It looks like we have a weather window of about a week, followed by a significant intensification of the wind,” leader Andrei Vasiliev told Anna Piunova of Mountain Club.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that it’s now or never for the Russian team on the West Ridge of Everest. Andrey Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov have set off for the summit without oxygen, hoping the weather will hold. They are completely alone on the mountain, and the push is full of risk.

In a recent development, everest is still loaded with fresh snow after two cyclones, and there are only three of them to break trail and find the best route above 7,500m. That was their highest point during their earlier venture in October. In addition, the wind may rise dramatically on Thursday, Vitor Baia, a Portuguese high-altitude meteorologist, told ExplorersWeb.

“It looks like we have a weather window of about a week, followed by a significant intensification of the wind,” leader Andrei Vasiliev told Anna Piunova of Mountain Club.

The question is exactly when the wind will increase, and whether the climbers will have enough time to summit and descend to a safer altitude.

“They have three days of weak wind, until Wednesday [November 11], but then the wind will increase sharply,” noted Baia.

Industry observers note that he says the best summit day will be Tuesday, with clear skies and weak winds. “Then they could use Wednesday to descend,” he added. “[That day will have] some clouds but still acceptable wind speeds.”.

The situation will worsen remarkably on Thursday, when the wind will shift from the west to the northwest and increase dramatically to 50 kph at 8,000m and 60kph at the summit.

In addition, avalanche hazards are still high due to the large amounts of snow after the latest storm two weeks ago. Finally, as winter approaches, it’s getting colder every day, the climbers reported.

After their first trip up ended in a tactical retreat as the cyclone hit, they retreated to Kathmandu to recover from some health concerns. Now they are fit again and ready for a second try. They returned to Base Camp last Thursday. Not surprisingly, they found it covered in a thick upcoming layer of snow. Breaking trail, they sank at some points up to their waists, Vasiliev reported.

Sources indicate that “Our high-altitude boots were in a cache two hours ahead of us, so we used duct tape to seal our pant cuffs to our trekking boots, trying to keep the snow out,” Kondrashkin reported. They eventually reached the cache and continued up in an exhausting 14-hour-long effort to a second cache (their Camp 1), where they had left their tent and sleeping bags.

They were near an avalanche-prone area and several snow slides swept nearby, prompting them to wait a day before continuing. Meanwhile, Shipilov indicated signs of food poisoning. Kodrashkin recalls that Saturday morning started with the following conversation:.

I wake up at 4:00 to boil some water.

“Vitalya, how are you feeling? Are we heading up?”.

Sources indicate that that answer needs some clarification. A professional like Vitaly Viktorovich [Shipilov] really only has two modes: “We’re going” and “I’m dying.”.

In fact, Shipilov had a fever and acute pain in the lower back, so the team headed down to their base in Lobuche. As this was going on, the snow had time to sluff off from the previously avalanche-prone area.

In a recent development, after just one night of rest, Vasiliev confirmed they were going up again. If all went according to plan, they will spend tonight back in their tent above the Lho La. Unfortunately, the climbers have not shared their tracker showing their current location and progress. On their previous trip up, they reached some 7,500m on Everest’s West Shoulder, near the beginning of the West Ridge and the potential detour to the Hornbein Couloir.

Winners of the Banff Mountain Film Festival Declared

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (800 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the annual Banff Centre Mountain Festival gathers mountain luminaries from across the world at the Banff Centre for Arts and Creativity in Alberta.
  • Industry observers note that the Grand Prize went to Listen, directed by Taliesin Black-Brown.
  • Rose Bush, an Oscar Award-winning director of photography serving on the competition’s jury, called Listen “a film that engages human-caused environmental devastation — the existential dilemma of our time — at its nucleus with overwhelming love and hope.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the annual Banff Centre Mountain Festival gathers mountain luminaries from across the world at the Banff Centre for Arts and Creativity in Alberta. There, a celebration of mountain culture recognizes the best outdoor films and books of the past year. The climax of the festival took place this past weekend, and the winners of the 51st annual Banff Mountain Film Competition have now been announced.

Industry observers note that the Grand Prize went to Listen, directed by Taliesin Black-Brown. In this short documentary, sound engineer Hank Lentfer records the sounds of nature around his Alaska home, while caring for his mother with dementia. As Lentfer documents the degradation of the natural world, we witness the slow loss of his mother. Drawing together these two threads, the film explores connection despite, and through, loss, using sound.

Rose Bush, an Oscar Award-winning director of photography serving on the competition’s jury, called Listen “a film that engages human-caused environmental devastation — the existential dilemma of our time — at its nucleus with overwhelming love and hope.”.

The film also won the Grand Jury Prize at the Tribeca Film Festival.

Sources indicate that in addition to a grand prize, the festival honors films in several categories. The winning film in the Adventure category was The Navigator, a feature-length work from director Jordan Manley. The film follows Nainoa Thompson, who was the first Native Hawaiian in six centuries to make the journey from Hawaii to Tahiti in a traditional voyaging canoe. Now, almost five decades later, Thompson and his crew make the journey again, using only traditional navigation techniques.

It has been revealed that the best film in the Mountain Culture category was Land of Canaan, produced and directed by Maggie Lemere. Lemere’s film follows a group of Palestinian olive farmers, who work to protect their ancient olive groves amid the destruction by Israel. The film “illuminated the vital relationship of courage, vision, hope, and traditional ecological knowledge,” juror Rose Bush noted, “in service of the essential value of sovereignty via mountain culture.”.

In the Environment category, director James Dawson’s winning comedic documentary Derek vs Derek follows two Devon farmers, both named Derek. One Derek is an ardent dairy farmer while his environmentalist neighbor begins rewilding his land. A feud naturally ensues.

The Arc’teryx-sponsored Best Climbing Film was Zindabad, directed by Tom Fish. Fish follows Pakistani climber Mueez Ud Din into the Karakoram, alongside his uncle Javed Ali and French climber Mathieu Maynadier. Ud Din explores a remote, unknown glacier system, while the film examines what it means to be a Pakistani climber among peaks long claimed by international outsiders.

It has been revealed that directed by Alexis Berg, the Mountain Sports winner, Roots, follows trail runner Ruth Croft as she examines her future as an elite ultra-trail runner after an injury. Roots is “about an inner journey of healing and acceptance, rooted in the essential joy of running outdoors,” explained juror David Arnaud.

Sources indicate that the Snow Sports winner centers on American skier Jessie Diggins. Diggins is the most decorated American cross-country skier ever, but Threshold, directed by Torsten Brinkema, reveals the deep personal struggles behind that success. Juror Beki Henderson noted that “the jury particularly commends Jessie Diggins for her extraordinary courage and honesty in sharing her story.”.

Industry observers note that there were more mountain films this year than you can even imagine. With 610 film submissions and 83 finalists, it’s no wonder that there are still more category winners.

Best short film winner Hello, Beautiful follows climber Alannah Yip as she struggles with identity, training for the Olympics while enduring medical hair loss. Director Darcy Hennessey created a film which “reminds us that personal transformation does not always come from pushing harder,” juror Kerry Stauffer explained.

Industry observers note that for best feature film, the competition revealed Ceremony, directed and produced by Banchi Hanuse. The film tells the story of the disappearance of the ooligan, a small fish, from British Columbia’s Bella Coola River. Jurors praised the film’s use of watercolor animation, personal stories, and community broadcasts to explore the importance of a seemingly unimportant little fish.

Director Marco Tribelhorn’s 75 seconds won the Creative Excellence Award. The film documents free-skier Jacob Wester’s 75-second-long battle for survival while trapped in an avalanche.

“A compelling visual treatment brings to life an experience that is impossible to imagine,” said Kerry Stauffer.

According to recent reports, last but not least, the Audience Choice Award went to Only Music // Snake River. Director Justin Fountain’s documentary follows a band that ditches the tour bus for a journey down the Snake River, seeking connection with strangers.

Tickets for the international film festival are now available. We have also covered the recently declared Banff Mountain Book Award winners.

Latest Update: A 3,300Km Walk Across Japan in Winter

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (467 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Japanese publisher Katsunari Tanaka has set himself the challenge of hauling a handcart 3,345km from Japan’s northernmost tip to the southern edge of Okinawa in winter.
  • Tanaka, 49, set off from Cape Sōya in Hokkaido on October 7 and is heading south to Cape Hedo in Okinawa.
  • Rather than carrying everything on his back, he is pulling a handcart that weighs around 100kg.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Japanese publisher Katsunari Tanaka has set himself the challenge of hauling a handcart 3,345km from Japan’s northernmost tip to the southern edge of Okinawa in winter.

Tanaka, 49, set off from Cape Sōya in Hokkaido on October 7 and is heading south to Cape Hedo in Okinawa. He hopes to complete the traverse in 100 days over five months. As he will have to contend with some challenging winter conditions along the way, he has described it as “playing chase with winter.”.

Rather than carrying everything on his back, he is pulling a handcart that weighs around 100kg. He also has a support team with a vehicle in case of emergencies. At some points, different members of his team have walked with him for a day or so. His daily target is around 35km, with rest days and organized stops built into the schedule.

The first few weeks have already brought strong headwinds, rain, and some steep climbs, making progress difficult at times. Temperatures have dropped close to freezing. At the end of October, he crossed a mountain pass between Yoichi and Iwanai. There, headwinds stirred up the gravel as he walked. Then the snow began. In the end, he took refuge with his support team until the weather improved.

Despite the conditions, Tanaka reached Hakodate Harbor on November 3, having covered 621km across Hokkaido. From Hakodate, he is crossing the Tsugaru Strait by ferry to Aomori, then will continue south along the Sanriku coast to Sendai.

It has been revealed that from there, he follows the Pacific coast through Fukushima to Tokyo before joining the Tokaido route toward Osaka before heading west to Kyushu. A second ferry crossing brings him to Okinawa, where he will walk to his final destination, Cape Hedo.

Along a road in Hokkaido. Photo: Katsunari Tanaka/Instagram.

This is not Tanaka’s first experience of traveling Japan with a handcart. Around a decade ago, he spent three years visiting all 47 prefectures, selling books directly to people he met along the way. Loading his publications onto a cart, he covered the country between 2013 and 2016, eventually selling 13,477 books. At the time, many people questioned what he was doing and whether books could really be sold on the street. But he notes the experience shaped his approach to business and his belief in the power of personal connections.

Tanaka insists that he is not an adventurer. Instead, he is traveling the country as a “merchant.” This time, he is making the journey to support his mentor, Arthur Hollands, a Japanese evangelist known for undertaking lengthy walks while carrying a large wooden cross. Along the route, Tanaka aims to stop at 11 locations to give lectures. He welcomes people to join him for sections of the walk.

Photo: Katsunari Tanaka/Instagram.

#125283. First Ski Descent of Meru Central

First Ski Descent of Meru Central

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (402 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tiphaine Duperier and Boris Langenstein of France have notched another Himalayan first ski descent, this time down the southwest face of Meru Central (6,310m) in India’s Garhwal Himalaya.
  • Duperier admitted they started the expedition with low expectations after several projects earlier in the fall all failed.
  • According to recent reports, “Snow conditions had been unforgiving,” she wrote.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tiphaine Duperier and Boris Langenstein of France have notched another Himalayan first ski descent, this time down the southwest face of Meru Central (6,310m) in India’s Garhwal Himalaya. The skiers are still surprised by how lucky they were.

Duperier admitted they started the expedition with low expectations after several projects earlier in the fall all failed.

According to recent reports, “Snow conditions had been unforgiving,” she wrote. “We figured there was only a 3-in-10 chance of skiing the southwest face of Meru.”.

But when they got there, the mountain was, they added, “generous” with them.

The three-peaked Meru massif, located in the Gangotri Glacier region of the Garhwal Himalaya, lies between Shivling and Thalay Sagar. It has three peaks: 6,660m Meru South, 6,310m Meru Central, and 6,450m Meru North. The ski descent line is in purple. Photo: Duperier/Langenstein.

“We spent six days of reconnaissance and three [days] climbing the peak, [thanks to] an unprecedented stroke of luck in finding a way through the icefall and perfect snow in the upper section,” she explained.

The icefall on Meru Central. Photo: Boris Langenstein.

It has been revealed that the icefall at the base of the peak was indeed one of the most complex passages. The pair climbed a 15m pitch of WI4 and left a safety rope, which they also used to rappel down after the ski descent, Duperier told PlanetMountain.

Otherwise, the pair of regular expedition and skiing partners climbed alpine-style and pretty fast, reaching the summit in less than eight hours. According to their research, they completed the second-ever ascent of the southwest face of Meru, after an Indian team in 2023.

At the summit on Meru Central. Photo: Duperier/Langenstein.

The skiers estimate they covered 1,500m on their descent, with some sections reaching 50 °. Snow conditions were good overall, hard but with a good grip.

“We skied like little monkeys on the wires in Rishikesh,” Duperier posted on social media. “It was just incredible, truly beautiful!”.

While the climbers rappelled down the icefall onto the glacier below, the ski descent itself had no rappels or interruptions.

Duperier barely had time to return home to France to pick up a Piolet d’Or for the first alpine-style ascent of the Schell Route on the Rupal Face of Nanga Parbat, followed by the first ski descent from the 8,125m summit.

Tiphaine Duperier at the Piolets d’Or ceremony. Photo: Piotr Drozdz.

#125281. The 2026 Appalachian Trail Thru-Hiker Survey: General Information (Part 1)

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3557 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

The 2026 Appalachian Trail Thru-Hiker Survey: General Information (Part 1)

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3557 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, each year, The Trek asks all Appalachian Trail hikers to complete a survey about their hike preparation, trail experiences, and personal backpacking journeys.
  • Sources indicate that our hope is that this survey serves as a great resource for prospective Appalachian Trail thru-hikers as they strategy and prepare for their hike.
  • A note on the data: As this survey is intended to help prospective thru-hikers plan for the trail, we filter the responses to only include those who either initially planned to complete the entire trail or those who hiked enough on the trail to have pertinent statistics to thru-hikers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, each year, The Trek asks all Appalachian Trail hikers to complete a survey about their hike preparation, trail experiences, and personal backpacking journeys. We’ve taken all the information from our 293 responses this year and have analyzed it to help you better understand the Appalachian Trail Class of 2026.

Sources indicate that our hope is that this survey serves as a great resource for prospective Appalachian Trail thru-hikers as they strategy and prepare for their hike. However, please keep in mind that no two hikes look the same, and you should by no means feel obligated to follow the trends or “averages” presented here. Use this data as a guide to inform your decisions, but remember that the most successful hike is the one that works best for you.

A note on the data: As this survey is intended to help prospective thru-hikers plan for the trail, we filter the responses to only include those who either initially planned to complete the entire trail or those who hiked enough on the trail to have pertinent statistics to thru-hikers.

We therefore excluded responses from hikers who hiked less than 500 miles and never intended to thru-hike; those who intended to complete an AT thru-hike but needed to stop before hiking 500 miles are still included. If you have any feedback on this benchmark, please leave a comment and let us know what you think the cutoff should be for 2027.

Using this framework, we have collected data from 294 AT long-distance hikers in 2026. The number will rise as we continue to accept responses from southbound hikers, and this survey will be updated with their information later into 2027.

This first post will focus on the broader demographics and logistics for Appalachian Trail hikers, while the next post will dig into the on-trail experiences and favorites/least favorites of this year’s Class.

AT Thru-Hiker Demographics Prior Experience, Injuries, and Completion Rates Direction, Start and Finish Dates, and Pace Budget.

The age distribution of hikers starting the trail remains generally consistent year over year, though 2026 pushed the upper boundaries of the age range even further. This season, our youngest hiker was 16 years old, while at the other end of the spectrum, the oldest hiker was 76. (For comparison, the 2025 range spanned from 12 to 73, and 2024 ran from 18 to 71.).

Notably, though he did not fill out our survey, Dale “Grey Beard” Sanders was the oldest thru-hiker on trail this year, setting the age record for an Appalachian Trail thru-hike at 91.

It has been revealed that we continue to see a large core group of hikers in their 20s and early 30s. These are typically recent college graduates and those unburdened by mortgage or family ties. This group is followed by another notable wave of hikers in their late 50s and early 60s, as retirees use their extra time and financial stability to take on the trail.

This year, the average age of an AT thru-hiker was 39, which remains much higher than the most commonly reported age of 25. In statistics, when the mean (39) sits well above the median (34) and mode (25), it points to a long tail end of older participants pulling the overall average upward.

READ NEXT: The Appalachian Trail Thru-Hiker Survey: All Years.

Since The Trek began collecting demographic data for the survey in 2016, the gender distribution has fluctuated between around 54 and 63% men. In 2025, 63% of survey respondents were men, which was the highest proportion of men to date.

This year, we stay consistent with that high proportion of men at 62.5%, while responses from women rose slightly to 34.8% and non-binary respondents held steady at just over 2%.

The trail remains overwhelmingly (96%) White, a trend that persists year over year as the proportion of White respondents has consistently landed above 90% since we began collecting demographic data in 2016.

While efforts to diversify the outdoors continue, the demographic data demonstrates that hikers identifying as White still make up the overwhelming majority, with fewer than 4% of hikers identifying as Hispanic, Asian, Black, Native American, or Pacific Islander. This number, while already small, is even smaller than in 2025, when we saw just over 4% of hikers identifying as non-White.

Sources indicate that as with previous years, the vast majority of survey respondents in 2026 (90%) were from the United States. Eleven other countries were represented among the respondents, which is slightly more than we saw last year, with international hikers primarily coming from Canada, the UK, and Germany.

Within the United States, the majority of hikers continued to hail from eastern and Mid-Atlantic states, taking advantage of closer geographic proximity to the trail.

As in previous years, we hypothesize that hikers from eastern states are more likely to tackle the AT due to easier travel logistics and greater familiarity and emotional connection with the area. Last year, Colorado marked the non-eastern state with the most respondents; this year, only 6 responses came from Colorado while Ohio and Texas each produced 10.

The states producing the most respondents this year were North Carolina, Pennsylvania, and Virginia, tied for the top spot with 21 respondents each and closely followed by Georgia at 15 — all states found along the Appalachian Trail.

Education levels remained consistent with previous years — our survey indicates that Appalachian Trail thru-hikers continue to be a highly educated group, with two-thirds of respondents holding a Bachelor’s, graduate, or professional degree.

Similar to prior years, the small fraction of respondents indicating they did not finish high school is largely (though not entirely) accounted for by younger hikers who took on the trail as recent graduates or during gap periods.

This year, respondents hailed from over 200 distinct occupations before starting the trail. We’ve grouped them into the above categories, with STEM & Professional Services (Engineering, Technology, Science, Finance, Law, and Corporate Administration) once again leading the pack at 35.4% of responses.

Sources indicate that students and educators continue to make up a significant segment of the thru-hiking community. Educators alone account for 5.5% of respondents. When we asked participants how they secured the time off to thru-hike, 7.3% of respondents cited having summers off or seasonal flexibility, while another 6.9% leveraged scheduled breaks from school.

According to recent reports, as in prior years, nearly 38.1% of respondents quit their jobs entirely to hike. Combined with the 23.2% who are retired, career breaks, transitions, and retirement make up over 60% of the total AT Class of 2026, showing how much a long-distance trail can stem from or cause a major life pivot.

Industry observers note that the average hiker on the Appalachian Trail in 2026 had between one and seven nights of prior backpacking experience, with nearly 30% of respondents falling into the 1-to-3-nights bracket and over 21% falling into the 4-to-7-nights range. Very few respondents reported having no prior hiking or backpacking experience at all. Meanwhile, a strong group (13.3%) reported 3 months or more of prior experience, likely representing hikers who had previously completed other long-distance trails.

This year, we also examined the rates of unplanned early exits from trail across these prior experience levels. Interestingly, the data highlights that prior backpacking experience does not strictly dictate success; hikers with modest experience (such as 1-3 nights or 4-7 nights) experienced relatively stable and moderate rates of not finishing (23% and 23.4%, respectively).

It has been revealed that those with zero prior backpacking experience did face a higher-than-average attrition rate (31.6% for day hikers only and 50% for the two hikers who reported never hiking or camping, for what that tiny dataset is worth). Overall, though, the data continues to corroborate the idea that the Appalachian Trail can successfully be a first major thru-hike for well-prepared beginners.

This year, 73.9% of survey respondents completed thru-hikes with over 2,000 miles hiked, rebounding nicely from last year’s rate of 63.7% and surpassing the 71% mark reported in 2024.

Industry observers note that however, this continues to trend much higher than the completion rates reported by the Appalachian Trail Conservancy (ATC), which historically hovers around a 25% to 30% success rate. There are a few key reasons for this consistent disparity.

Sources indicate that first, the ATC captures a massive dataset of every registered start, whereas our survey relies on voluntary responses. Second, because we promote our survey through The Trek and our Instagram and community channels, we naturally attract responses from hikers who are plugged into the thru-hiking ecosystem and are often better equipped and more motivated to finish.

Recent findings suggest that we speculate that readers of The Trek are simply better prepared for the physical and mental demands of the trail after engaging with our guides and community. While we can’t prove that our content is the secret sauce to a successful AT thru-hike, please let us keep believing it for the sake of our ego.

According to recent reports, 75 survey respondents this year did not complete a full thru-hike. Of that group, 13.3% (10 hikers) stated they only intended to hike a section or had already reached their personal mileage goal. That represents a sharp decline from 2025, when planned section hikers accounted for 39% of the non-finishing respondents (likely because we worked harder to filter out short-distance section hikers from the dataset this year).

When we look at the 65 hikers who experienced an unplanned exit from the trail, injury remains the undisputed primary reason, accounting for 38.7% of all non-finishers. Tying for the next most common reasons were family/personal obligations and mental burnout (such as boredom or loss of motivation), each accounting for 13.3% of respondents who left the trail.

Interestingly, while 2025 was an anomaly where zero respondents cited finances as their reason for leaving the trail, money troubles returned in 2026: running out of funds accounted for 8% of exits (6 hikers), tying with illness and the general physical toll of the trail.

One key note about this data: though we advertise this survey to the best of our ability, many hikers who unexpectedly left the trail early are likely not engaging with Appalachian Trail media by the time autumn rolls around. As a result, our responses remain skewed toward those who completed their hikes as planned, meaning we are likely only seeing a partial picture of trail attrition.

According to recent reports, not only were injuries the largest cause of needing to leave the trail, but they were also quite pervasive among all the hikers on trail. More than half of our survey respondents (55.4%) experienced an injury during their 2026 hike, while 44.6% made it through unscathed.

Getting hurt on the Appalachian Trail does not automatically mean the end of the trail. Over 81% of injured hikers managed to stay on the trail by adapting their routine. Nearly a third of those injured (32.5%) hiked through the pain without taking any time off. Another 28.1% dialed back their daily mileage to recover, while 20.6% took some time off the trail.

Ultimately, 18.8% of reported injuries were hike-ending (9.9% of all respondents).

In 2026, hike direction returned to its traditional pre-Hurricane Helene baseline, with the proportion of Northbound hikers jumping nearly 13 percentage points to 92.9% (up from 80.2% in 2025). Conversely, Flip-Flop hikes dropped from 13.5% to 5.0%, and Southbound respondents fell from 6.3% to 2.1%.

Industry observers note that that shift confirms last year’s spike in alternative itineraries was largely a temporary response to Hurricane Helene. Ahead of the 2025 season, the ATC and media outlets (like us!) encouraged hikers to pursue Southbound or Flip-Flop hikes to give southern trail towns and trail crews time to rebuild. With the southern portion of the trail recovered and reopened for the 2026 season, the vast majority of thru-hikers returned to the classic Georgia-to-Maine route.

Despite expectations last year that Southbound numbers would continue to climb as more people learned about the benefits of hiking south, the pull of the traditional Northbound social bubble remains hard to beat.

Most hikers began their hikes in March and April (accounting for nearly 75% of all start dates), with the single most popular start date this year shifting about two weeks earlier to March 14, closely followed by March 9.

We asked respondents if they were satisfied with their start dates, and satisfaction jumped even higher this year: 94% of all respondents reported being happy with when they set out. Because the 2026 bubble shifted slightly earlier into March, the average start date for satisfied NOBO hikers moved up to March 18 (compared to March 29 in 2025).

Meanwhile, the average start date for NOBO hikers who felt they started too early was February 12, while the average date for those who felt they started too late fell between April 8 and April 10. With over 9 out of 10 hikers satisfied with their choice, the “right” start date ultimately comes down to the type of trail experience you want to have.

The small handful of hikers who felt they started too late cited weather concerns, wanting a slower pace during the first few weeks, not having enough time to heal from an injury and still finish, or feeling stressed as a solo hiker at the tail end of the bubble. Conversely, the five hikers who felt they started too early pointed to cold winter weather in February and early March. One April 6 starter noted they actually wished the trail had been more crowded.

If you want to start in what most thru-hikers consider the “sweet spot” for Northbounders, aim for a mid-to-late March window, keeping in mind that starting right in the March bubble means sharing shelters and campsites with bigger crowds early on.

Southbound hikers start later in the season — this year ranging from May 29 to August 12, with most setting out in late May and June — to let winter conditions clear up north. All eight of our current Southbound respondents reported being satisfied with their start dates, though the sample size remains too small to track broader date trends.

This year we’re keeping the survey open for Southbound applicants who are still on trail, and we’ll be back with more SOBO data early in 2027. SOBOs: click here to take the 2026 Appalachian Trail Thru-Hiker Survey.

Recent findings suggest that most successful thru-hikers finish between mid-July and mid-October, with September (86 hikers) and August (65 hikers) as the peak months for summiting Katahdin. The single most popular finish date this year was September 15 (9 hikers), closely followed by September 19 and August 26.

While a small handful of fast-moving Northbounders finished as early as late May and June — led by one early starter who wrapped up on May 31 and noted it was too early for weather-related reasons — the vast majority timed their finishes for late summer and early autumn, well within Baxter State Park’s typical May-to-October operating window.

According to recent reports, overall, 94.4% of thru-hikers reported being satisfied with their finish date. The average finish date that Northbound hikers were satisfied with was August 27 (shifting a little over two weeks later than last year’s August 11 average), while the average finish date reported as too late for weather-related reasons was September 10 for Northbounders. Two Northbound hikers who summited on September 19 and September 20 felt their finish dates were too crowded, landing right in the heart of the mid-September summit bubble.

In a recent development, with the information on start and end dates, we can look at the duration and pacing of hikers’ treks. We filtered this data to only include respondents who completed a thru-hike of the Appalachian Trail.

According to recent reports, the average completed thru-hike this year took 160 days (just over five months), ticking up slightly from last year’s 153-day average. The longest reported thru-hike was 230 days (a flip-flopper who started February 27 and finished October 12), while the fastest completed thru-hike was an 88-day Southbound trek, followed closely by two Northbounders who finished in 96 days.

It has been revealed that we also asked self-reported thru-hikers about their average daily mileage, with the overall average across respondents coming in at 15.0 miles per day (up from 14.3 miles per day in 2025). The single most-reported daily mileage was once again 15 miles per day (31 hikers), followed closely by 14 and 13 miles per day.

Industry observers note that even though our survey asks hikers to include zero days in their estimate, many respondents likely reported their hiking-day average rather than their true calendar average, or simply guessed without tracking exact daily numbers. Treat this figure as a loose ballpark: at the trail’s official length of 2,197.9 miles, the average 160-day thru-hike works out to a true calendar pace of roughly 13.7 miles per day once zero days and town stops are factored in.

In a recent development, attendance at trail festivals rebounded strongly in 2026, driven by a return to classic Northbound traffic and high engagement among thru-hikers. While 44.2% of survey respondents still reported not attending any trail festival, that figure dropped significantly from 2025 (when 56% reported no festival attendance) as crowds returned to trail towns.

According to recent reports, trail Days in Damascus, Virginia remains by far the most popular AT festival, with 44.2% of respondents attending. Meanwhile, the Northbound Kickoff at Amicalola Falls saw a significant attendance bump, drawing 11.6% of respondents.

Unlike in prior years, we filtered our financial questions to include only those who completed their thru-hikes, to better reflect how much it actually costs to hike the entire trail.

Likely in part due to this decision, the average cost of an Appalachian Trail thru-hike (including the cost of gear) climbed notably this year to $8,863 (compared to $7,680 in 2025 and $7,602 in 2024), with a median spend of $8,500 and many hikers reporting total costs exceeding $10,000.

Industry observers note that the spread of hikers across the cost spectrum demonstrates significant spikes around $6,000 and $8,000, along with 28 hikers reporting spending $10,000. At the extreme ends, only 6 hikers reported spending under $2,500, while 15 reported spending $15,000 or more.

Hikers spent an average of $2,305 on their gear in 2026 across all respondents who completed 500 miles or more on the AT, ticking up moderately from previous years. The median gear spend was $2,000, with the most common spending bracket also at $2,000 (57 hikers).

The vast majority of hikers spent under $4,000 on their gear, which covers the initial cost of purchasing packs, tents, and sleep systems along with the ongoing replacement or repair of footwear, clothing, and worn-out items over the course of their journey.

While most kept their setups budget-friendly or mid-tier with their spend peaking between $1,000 and $2,500, a few outliers scaled the high end of the luxury spectrum, with 11 respondents reporting gear investments exceeding $10,000 (including two hikers topping out at $11,000).

Industry observers note that to those few hikers who absolutely splurged, shoot me a message. I’d love to know what on earth is in your pack.

We’re stopping here for now, but there is plenty more data to come. In the next few posts, we will break down everything from hiker experience levels and safety concerns to the nitty-gritty gear stats on shelters, footwear, and backpacks.

Looking for other years? Find every Trek AT thru-hiker survey on our Appalachian Trail Thru-Hiker Survey page.

I'm Katie, a thru-hiker and ultrarunner based in Colorado. After thru-hiking the Colorado Trail, John Muir Trail, Continental Divide Trail, and Long Trail in back-to-back years, I'm looking forward to a little time of rest, relaxation, and hanging out with my cat. Or, who knows, maybe the AT. No one has ever accused me of being good at sitting still.

Industry observers note that I’m planning my NOBO and these surveys are tremendously helpful! Also lol that there were no 37 year old hikers.

Recent findings suggest that I’m so glad to hear it! I’m also stoked this year to be able to come back and include more information on SOBO hikes as we get those responses finalized. We need a 37 year old out there next year.

Seems a little premature since 2026 is not over. People finish at all times of the year and deserve to have their experiences recorded.

According to recent reports, I agree! That’s why we’re getting the survey out now (to support those planning to start their 2027 hikes right at the New Year) and will continue to upgrade this article with information from SOBO and section hikers who continue to finish their hikes into the end of the year!

Tech Report: Arctic Town Kills Dozens of Grizzlies Feeding on Dump

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that for years, the grizzlies near Inuvik in Canada’s western Arctic relied on a stable source of food — the town dump.
  • In 2025, before the fence was built, trail cameras captured multiple grizzlies hanging around the dump, looking for food.
  • Sources indicate that it was too much.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that for years, the grizzlies near Inuvik in Canada’s western Arctic relied on a stable source of food — the town dump. Generations of bears grew up feeding there. In 2025, wildlife officials found that over 40 grizzlies regularly visited the dump.

In 2025, before the fence was built, trail cameras captured multiple grizzlies hanging around the dump, looking for food. Photo: Government of the Northwest Territories.

Sources indicate that it was too much. This year, the town built an electric fence around the site, hoping the bears would move on. They didn’t. Some started coming into town looking for food. Others just hung around the fence, searching for a way in.

Industry observers note that “They would just do these laps around the dump, and they would just be emaciated, sickly,” stated Toby Halle, a Renewable Resources officer based in Inuvik, told the CBC. “They don’t know what to do with themselves. And quite frankly, we don’t know what to do with them.”.

According to recent reports, inuvik, population about 3,500, was the first community in that part of the Arctic to try to wean the bears off their dependence on dump food with such a fence, which cost about $700,000. The problem was, the bears had not learned to depend on any other source of food.

According to recent reports, “We’ve probably had three to four generations of bears that have been using that landfill,” stated local mayor Peter Clarkson. In the end, the town took a drastic solution — but one that was probably unavoidable in the circumstances: They shot 28 bears.

Tragic though this is, officials hope that within the next couple of years, the remaining bears in the area will move on and learn to eat more natural fare.

Recent findings suggest that many other Arctic towns still have open dumps where bears come to feed. Photo: Government of the Northwest Territories.
