#125275. Leonard Clark: Explorer, Spy, Liar

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2563 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Leonard Clark: Explorer, Spy, Liar

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2563 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Born in 1907, Leonard Francis Clark was an explorer, war hero, and writer who made daring expeditions all over the world before dying mysteriously in Venezuela in 1957.
  • It has been revealed that today, he isn’t well known, but has this lack of scrutiny been a blessing in disguise for this forgotten explorer’s legacy?
  • Sources indicate that A Tibetan expedition under Leonard Clark in 1949.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Born in 1907, Leonard Francis Clark was an explorer, war hero, and writer who made daring expeditions all over the world before dying mysteriously in Venezuela in 1957.

It has been revealed that today, he isn’t well known, but has this lack of scrutiny been a blessing in disguise for this forgotten explorer’s legacy? His books, filled with adventure and excitement, read like fiction. The more one digs into the forgotten reports and old newspaper articles, the stranger his story, and the more complicated the man.

Sources indicate that A Tibetan expedition under Leonard Clark in 1949. Photo: The Marching Wind.

According to recent reports, the main sources on Leonard Clark are all, well, Leonard Clark. This isn’t necessarily damning, but it is something he shares with most good con artists or cult leaders. The following is a short biography based only on official records, such as draft cards and census data. The first rule of reading historical accounts is that every historical figure is a liar.

Leonard Francis Clark was born in British Columbia, Canada, in January 1907 to two Americans, Maud and Francis Clark. In 1909, they moved back to Maud’s birth state of California, and Francis promptly died.

There are conflicting statements online about which university he attended, but census data shows him living only a few kilometers from the University of California (now the University of California, Berkeley) in 1930, so I’d put my money on that one. He began traveling right out of college, spending three years in Borneo on a hunting trip with his brother, Laurence. By the late 1930s, he was on a National Geographic-funded expedition to the South China Sea.

Photo: National Geographic Archives.

His article, cryptically titled Among the Significant Knot Lois of Hainan, was published in the 1938 September edition. In it, he recounts how he and a small expeditionary force landed in the midst of a deadly cholera epidemic. Relying on hired porters to carry their supplies, Clark and Nicol Smith, another future travel writer, set off into the interior. Soon, malaria and infection laid low most of the team, including, per Clark’s article, Smith.

Again, according to Clark, Smith urged him to take the remaining five porters, the minimum of equipment, and keep going.

Recent findings suggest that much of the article is dedicated to ethnographic observations, with the typical exoticism and patronizing tone of the era. At one point, Clark noted that the Li people of Hainan reminded him of indigenous Amazonian people and “the men were tall, many six feet.”.

Sources indicate that A recent study showed that the average height for men in Hainan today is 168.7cm, around 5’6″, and the same study found that average heights had increased over the past century. This is a small nitpick, but he’ll repeat this unlikely claim again in the Amazon. It is worth noting that the “six-foot-tall Indian warrior” was a stock character in contemporary pulp adventure fiction.

According to recent reports, there is an interesting contrast between Clark’s account and some of the newspaper reports, especially one from a Virginia paper, which relied on Smith for the story. This article implies Smith did much more than lay around his tent with malaria. Clark’s article claims he was the first white man to enter 47 different villages, while the newspaper claims that Smith was the first Westerner to penetrate inland.

Sources indicate that there is a third source: the 37-minute silent film compiled from the expedition’s footage and photographs. In it, we briefly see a white man lying under a mosquito net as if ill. But whether this is Smith, Clark — who admits himself to experiencing malaria symptoms on the expedition — or the third westerner on the expedition, one Jack Munroe, the film doesn’t say.

Photo: National Geographic Archive.

In a recent development, his previous experience in the region led him to return a few years later, this time on behalf of the U.S. Office of Strategic Services (OSS), a precursor to the CIA. His work during the war centered around the China-Burma-India corridor, particularly the Yellow River valley. He was involved in organizing guerrilla activities, building intelligence networks, and navigating the Japanese surrender of Taiwan.

In a recent development, in a later press statement, Clark explained how he had worked with General Dai Li, and that “the Reds had it in for him,” due to the infamously repressive actions Dai Li took against Chinese Communists. Dai Li, whom historian Barbara Tuchman called “China’s combination of Himmler and J. Edgar Hoover,” was killed in a 1946 plane crash. Wide speculation places the blame for this crash on either the Chinese Communist Party or the OSS. This would make things awkward for Clark a few years later.

Industry observers note that he continued his government work in the area after the Second World War, sliding right into the developing Cold War. In 1949, Clark led a large, well-funded expedition into Tibet.

It has been revealed that it would have gotten him in the history books if Leonard Clark identified a peak higher than Everest. Unfortunately for him, he didn’t. But he certainly proposed that he had, when he claimed that he’d surveyed Amne Machin and found it to be 9,040m high.

According to recent reports, amne Machin is not taller than Everest. Photo: Wikimedia Commons.

Clark published his account of the expedition years later, titled The Marching Wind. In it, he wrote with his typical style: daring escapes, stereotypically aggressive natives, and breezy adventure writing. What it did not contain was the data to support his claims.

As soon as he released his first report and measurements, geographers, geologists, and mountaineers pored over them. Bradford Washburn, a cartographer, photographer, and explorer, published a thorough examination of the surveying techniques and questionable results from Clark’s expedition.

A contemporary review in the Alpine Journal, commenting on his photographic evidence, wrote that “anything more unconvincing could hardly be imagined — yet, ostensibly…the mountain was the object of the expedition.” More on that “ostensibly” later. Suffice it to say, Clark’s estimate that Amne Machin could be almost 1,000m taller than Everest was not adopted by geographers at large.

Industry observers note that the review concluded that “it can hardly be wondered if mountaineers, whom Mr. Clark rather despises, cannot accept his results.”.

Clark blithely remarked that he had “some rather bulky complaints by mountain and other specialists,” but admitted subpar instruments made his results “indecisive.”.

Industry observers note that A surveying party including Clark, far right, taking observations of Amne Machin. Photo: The Marching Wind.

If he doesn’t seem too broken up, it may be because Amne Machin’s height wasn’t the main purpose of his trip. Clark was supported logistically and went on behalf of Ma Bufang, the fiercely anti-communist warlord ruling Qinghai, on the border of Tibet. Anticipating that he could not long hold out against the People’s Liberation Army, Clark proposed that his expedition would map a path of retreat. This would help Ma Bufang’s army cross into Tibet and continue their anti-Communist campaign from the mountains.

Clark envisioned Ma Bufang’s Qinghai, through Tibet, becoming “the bulwark against Red invasion of India.” Clark went on the expedition and did his mapping, but the PLA took Qinghai only months later, and Ma Bufang fled to Hong Kong.

Industry observers note that in his introduction to his book, Clark claims that the United States was unaware of his “very slight aid” to Ma Bufang and local anti-Communist guerrilla activities, and he involved himself with the Chinese Nationalist army “as a private American citizen.” If I were to say that I was skeptical of this claim, I would not be the first to do so. But that falls under speculation, so I will say only that I sent a Freedom of Information Act request to the CIA regarding Clark’s work in Tibet. However, the records were not forthcoming.

After returning from the mountains, Clark went to a wedding anniversary celebration in Canton, surrounded by his fellow Allied intelligence members and their set. Things got a little out of hand, and Clark soon found himself in a Cantonese jail with a bullet wound and two manslaughter charges.

Chinese Nationalist soldiers on Clark’s Tibetan expedition. Photo: The Marching Wind.

According to recent reports, the other two men involved were Harold Harris, an Englishman who died immediately, and Willard Freeman from Massachusetts, who died later from his injuries. Clark also sustained a gunshot wound, but had recovered sufficiently by late November to be moved from hospital to prison.

The three had been drinking together in Freeman’s home when, at about 4 am, servants reported hearing gunshots. Mrs. Maya Freeman entered the room at 10 am to find an odd and grisly scene. Harris, fully clothed, lay dead on Freeman’s bed with three gunshot wounds. Freeman, completely nude, was also lying on the bed, alive with two shots to the abdomen. Clark, in his underwear, was on a second bed, with a single gunshot to the chest. Furniture was overturned, indicating a fight, and all three were covered in scratches. The only weapon found was Clark’s .32 caliber pistol.

Later that month, the Canton District Court denied Clark’s bail request. The court, still trying to determine what exactly happened, focused on the widowed Maya Freeman. Interviewing her for hours, they attempted to make her confess to an affair with Clark. Both of them repeatedly denied it. Clark further denied that he had fired any of the six shots, though he didn’t name the shooter.

According to recent reports, clark’s brother contacted former OSS head General William Donovan, who rallied the State Department. Clark reportedly was concerned that if he wasn’t released before the city fell to the Communists, he would be tortured for information regarding Dai Li and OSS activities. The State Department investigated and, thanks to its intervention, Clark was released.

Clark’s legal troubles were splashed across newspapers worldwide. Photo: The Journal (Caldwell, Ohio) November 24, 1949.

In a recent development, what exactly happened in Freeman’s house that night? Was the dispute between the Allied Intelligence men personal, or professional? If the world were ever to find out, it wouldn’t be from Clark. Once freed, Clark returned to California and moved on to his next adventure. It was an ambitious one: Leonard Clark was going to discover the lost city of El Dorado.

It has been revealed that he had an old parchment map to the lost city, he claimed, which showed it lay in the upper reaches of Peru. Never mind that it had been pretty well established for over a century that El Dorado was a myth, following the efforts of explorers Alexander von Humboldt and Robert Schomburgk.

According to recent reports, clark’s resulting account, The Rivers Ran East, contains all the genre tropes you would expect from a fictional work in the same setting. Native Amazonians are ferocious cannibals who capture Clark and keep him in a poison snake pit, crocodiles can and must be lassoed (there are no crocodiles in Peru, only caimans, a type of alligator), and there is a beautiful lady explorer, Inez Pokorny, who is secretly part of a London-based international El Dorado-seeking organization. If this organization existed, I have found no trace of it outside of this book.

In a recent development, if I were to list every blatant impossibility in his account, we would be here for days, so I’ll just continue on one particular thread: Leonard Clark seems to have a very loose grasp of which animals are in Peru and how significant they are. At one point, he is blinded by a venom-spitting snake. There are three venom-spitting snake species, and none of them are in South America.

His 500-pound (227kg) boars must be peccaries, pig-like animals native to the Americas. The Amazon native white-lipped peccary tops out around 40kg, while the unconfirmed giant peccary still has only been estimated at 50kg. Likewise, his 12m-long pythons must be anacondas, which have a maximum recorded length of eight meters.

Clark claims to have found El Dorado. What he found was a group of Chicham people panning for gold, who traded some of it to Clark and Pokorny. According to his book, Clark traveled under the pretense of investigating botanical medicines, while actually searching for El Dorado.

In fact, as the El Dorado adventures on the page grew more and more ridiculous, I began to wonder if it were not the other way around. Here I have fully entered the realm of speculation. American corporations were, and still are, extremely interested in extracting resources from South America, including pharmaceuticals. In fact, Clark also reported success in this area, claiming to have identified over 60 native medicinals with commercial possibility — as well as Amazonian oil.

In praise of Clark’s work, Baron Wolfenegg, Director of Colonization for the Orient in Peru, accidentally said the quiet part out loud, stating he’d “learned much from this book that will help my work of colonizing this vast jungle.”.

On Peru’s Perené River. Photo: The Rivers Ran East.

It is practically gauche for explorers to die in their beds, and Clark, who seemed to mold his life to the shape of adventure stories, was no exception. Clark was in Venezuela in 1957, looking, he claimed, for diamond mines. He entered the Amazon basin, never to emerge again.

It has been revealed that one history of the OSS offhandedly mentions that Clark died with “two native arrows in his back.” I suspect the explorer’s penchant for sensationalism survived his death. Other contemporary reports describe Clark as having drowned when his canoe overturned.

As I pointed out earlier, most of the information on Clark’s expeditions came from Clark himself. Since he never returned, startlingly little information is available about his death at age 49.

In a recent development, the area around the Orinoco River in Venezuela is, in fact, rich in diamond deposits. Photo: Wikimedia Commons.

The line between fact and fiction is notoriously vague in much of the adventure travel genre. Is Herman Melville telling the full truth about his time spent on the island of Nuku Hiva? Did anyone actually complete the “Long Walk” out of a Soviet detention camp, which Slavomir Rawicz falsely claimed as his own tale? How much artistic license and embellishment is acceptable before exploration accounts become outright hoaxes?

I didn’t write this article with the goal of proving Leonard Clark a charlatan. It can hardly be denied that he really was going to these places, at the very least. But there are enough discrepancies and inaccuracies in his accounts to conclude that they should be taken with a grain of salt, and his treasure-hunting pseudo-archaeological tendencies make his anthropological findings, well, questionable.

As a contemporary New Yorker book critic put it, Clark had “the same gift, or weakness, for grandiose verbiage that got Marco Polo in trouble with his fellow Venetians.”.

The real story, and one which may never be fully disentangled, lies in why, exactly, Clark was doing his exploring. Somewhere between the romantic adventurer and the cynically colonialist spy using exploration as a guise for the extractive, violent enforcement of Western capitalist hegemony, lies the truth.

“Every explorer has two faces,” Clark wrote in the opening to The Rivers Ran East; “the secret one and the one he indicates to the world.”.

#125272. Latest Update: The Dane Steadman Interview: Hard Going and High Stakes in the Karakoram

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1385 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: The Dane Steadman Interview: Hard Going and High Stakes in the Karakoram

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1385 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There is much more to an expedition than summit or failure.
  • The one factor on the team’s side was the previous experience of Steadman and Cody Winckler.
  • Grant Stewart of Canada, the third member of the Sosbun Brakk team, is a skilled climber but was less familiar with the Karakoram.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There is much more to an expedition than summit or failure. In this exclusive interview, American climber Dane Steadman explains why his recent new route on Karakoram’s Sosbun Brakk (6,414m) “was much more difficult than the one on Yashkuk Sar, both on and off the mountain.” Strong words, considering that he and his partners were awarded a Piolet d’Or for Yashkuk Sar.

The one factor on the team’s side was the previous experience of Steadman and Cody Winckler. “It was our third trip, so we knew a lot more about climbing there,” Steadman said. Indeed, after Yashkuk Sar, Winckler and Steadman returned to Pakistan in 2025 and climbed two fresh routes with Blake Berghoff.

Grant Stewart of Canada, the third member of the Sosbun Brakk team, is a skilled climber but was less familiar with the Karakoram. His most remarkable climbs had taken place in Alaska and at home in the Canadian Rockies.

According to recent reports, bivy in an ice cave. Photo Dane Steadman.

Comparing the two epic climbs, Steadman highlighted the differences.

“The trip to Yashkuk Sar went incredibly smoothly. Getting there and acclimatizing was great. We had an amazing weather window for the climb. Nothing on it was exceptionally hard, and we did it on the first try, and the descent went without a hitch,” he said.

He explained that the hardest parts of that 2024 first ascent were their lack of experience and the uncertainty that came with it. An unexpected mishap also occurred during the climb itself: a snow mushroom collapsed above them, forcing them to change their ascent route halfway up.

“On the other hand,” Steadman went on, “almost everything about the Sosbun Brakk trip was hard: lost bags, sickness acclimatizing, massive storms beforehand and while on the mountain, hard climbing and route-finding, and a very difficult descent through terrible weather.”.

According to recent reports, the unclimbed north face of Sosbun Brakk. Photo: Dane Steadman.

Recent findings suggest that “[Overall,] on the Yashkuk trip, I think we felt for most of the time that we would be able to do it with only some moments of doubt here and there,” Steadman admitted. “On Sosbun, we thought much of the time that we wouldn’t be able to do it for all the reasons above. We were quite surprised [to succeed].”.

One unusual aspect of the Sosbun Brakk expedition was its dates. They went to Pakistan and climbed in early fall, two months later than the Karakoram’s typical July-August climbing season. Yet, Steadman says this was planned to account for the changing climate in the high ranges.

In a recent development, approaching the face. Photo: Dane Steadman.

“First, while the Karakoram doesn’t receive as much of the Indian monsoon as the main Himalaya, it is still a monsoonal climate, and I think (and have heard from many locals now) that the weather tends to be much better in the fall than in the summer,” he explained.

“Second, we were concerned about rockfall and generally unsafe conditions on the face, being relatively low and lacking in buttresses. We thought the colder temperatures would make things safer and increase the odds of finding good ice.

In a recent development, “Third, Grant was able to get time off in October more easily than earlier in September. In a perfect world, we probably would have gone one to two weeks earlier, but we worked with what we had.”.

Asked about other expeditions planning to visit the Pakistani mountains in the future, Steadman suggests that October could be a good time for certain climbs, but that September is also great. “This year, the weather was much less stable in September-October than I’ve experienced on my previous trips. Things got much snowier than normal for that time of year, [according to locals], but I think the weather was still better than through most of the summer.”.

It has been revealed that the team planned a single alpine-style push in the purest style. However, when they started on the route, they encountered an impassable hanging serac. They had to retreat and decide whether to try a totally different line or go home.

According to recent reports, the base camp crew. Photo: Dane Steadman.

The team decided to try a route to the right of the originally planned one. But how could they be sure they wouldn’t reach another dead end?

Steadman admitted it was difficult. “The line we ended up climbing was entirely hidden from view at our base camp and where we acclimatized,” he explained. “[It was] an east-facing gash on a north face, which we only saw from the northwest until we tried it. From all the views we had before the first attempt, the central line we first attempted appeared to be the only route that wouldn’t involve climbing huge walls of monolithic gneiss, as it followed ice streaks and sheets for a good amount of it, and only looked to have relatively short cruxes.

At the base, they discovered that a tiny but menacing serac hung over the center of the wall, threatening the lower half. (The upper half appeared protected by an overhanging rock wall above it.).

“So we shifted to a different line to the left, which looked much harder but possible, and planned to rejoin our intended line at mid-height, under the protection of the overhangs.

Sources indicate that that attempt didn’t so much dead-end as things compounded, forcing a retreat. “We were tired even on the approach from non-stop efforts to get there and acclimatize. We had some equipment issues, were moving slowly, and most of all, the climbing was damn hard,” he said.

Recent findings suggest that in the end, they chose to rappel down after a two-hour-plus lead climb on a pitch that hadn’t looked hard from below. Dusk was approaching; there was no bivy spot in sight, and they were only 300m up the 1,800m wall.

Sources indicate that “However, from our position on that attempt, we were able to see the right-trending, east-facing gash on the right side of the face, which was totally hidden by monolithic rock walls from all our previous vantage points,” he said. “So, after bailing, we felt like the central line would require fresh bodies, minds, and a huge weather window, but the right-hand line would be much more feasible.”.

According to recent reports, heading up. Photo: Dane Steadman.

The climbers rested for three days in base camp and then set off again. “We certainly felt that we could get shut down at any number of points, especially at the steep mushroom-choked chimney on the headwall below the junction with the northwest spur,” Steadman admitted. “But it seemed like there was a good chance we could do it, and, most importantly, we felt like we could bail from anywhere [if necessary].”.

The summit ridge of Sosbun Brakk after many tough decisions. Photo: Dane Steadman.

However, bailing would not be easy. “The lower part would involve rappelling off V-threads, he explained, and if they had to turn back below the headwall, they would need to rappel out right to an icefield.

In a recent development, route topo: line of ascent in red, line of descent in yellow. Photo: Steadman/Stewart.

Recent findings suggest that the trio summited on their fifth day on the wall, at 4 pm. Days were now short, and they still had a long, uncertain descent ahead. The descent began on the line of ascent, but eventually deviated to new terrain.

“We descended the upper half of our route, almost entirely rappelling down the northwest spur, with a little bit of downclimbing/traversing),” Steadman said.

It has been revealed that they then reached a point west of their ascent line, where the face was slightly smaller and more covered in permanent ice. “Then we rappelled straight down, diagonaling back left partway down to avoid some serac hazard.”.

In a recent development, descending in worsening weather. Photo: Dane Steadman.

Dane Steadman and Cody Winckler of the U.S., together with Grant Stewart of Canada, completed the first ascent of the north face of Sosbun Brakk (6,414m) in Pakistan’s Karakoram last month. The peak had been climbed only once before, by a Japanese team in 1981, from a different, milder side. The new 1,800m route includes difficulties of M7, WI5.

#125269. Breaking: Natural Wonders: Crowley Lake Columns

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1045 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Natural Wonders: Crowley Lake Columns

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1045 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It is low tide on Crowley Lake in Mono County, California.
  • In a recent development, crowley Lake is a man-made reservoir, administered by the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power.
  • Father Crowley made it his mission to bolster tourism in the area.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It is low tide on Crowley Lake in Mono County, California. The water is still, the trout abundant, and one or two kayakers paddle about, enjoying the lack of tourists. But as you walk along the shore, something out of place appears: spiral pillars and arches that seem left over from some ancient civilization.

In a recent development, crowley Lake is a man-made reservoir, administered by the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power. It was named after an important figure in the community, affectionately known as the Desert Padre. This beloved Catholic priest worked tirelessly to help a community that experienced water shortages throughout the 1920s and 1930s. Water from the nearby Owen Valley was diverted to Los Angeles, leaving very little for local residents.

Father Crowley made it his mission to bolster tourism in the area. The publicity led authorities to help locals by drawing up plans for a dam and reservoir. When Father Crowley died in a car accident, authorities completed the Long Valley Dam and named the reservoir Lake Crowley. If it weren’t for his intervention, the lake wouldn’t have existed.

According to recent reports, as the years passed, visitors continued coming to Lake Crowley to fish, kayak, camp, and hike. Then something weird started to appear on the cliffsides. The banks appeared to be receding and hollowing out, revealing hundreds upon hundreds of spiral columns. Many onlookers believed they were man-made. Some compared the formations to Moorish architecture from North Africa and Spain.

Though the reservoir is man-made, the area’s history dates back millennia. Crowley Lake lies in the wider Long Valley Caldera, one of Earth’s largest calderas.

According to recent reports, some of the columns. Photo: Shutterstock.

The caldera sits atop one of three ancient supervolcanoes in the United States. Around 760,000 years ago, this supervolcano erupted and spewed 650 cubic kilometers of rhyolite rock and ash into the air for a week. It covered the land in a blanket of ash and debris over one kilometer thick. And it left behind a 32km long, 18km wide, and 900m deep depression in the earth.

The depression formed when the subterranean magma chamber emptied onto the surface and the remnant shell of a roof collapsed. The blast and pyroclastic flow were so powerful that ash fell as far as Kansas. Along the rim are the lava dome complexes of Mammoth, Glass, and Bald Mountains. The caldera also hosts a cluster of hydrothermally active lakes called the Mammoth Lakes.

The main feature left by the eruption is the Bishop Tuff, a few square kilometers in area. A tuff is a rock of compacted volcanic ash. At the base of this tuff stand the Crowley Lake Columns. They range in thickness, average about six meters high, and are generally reddish, beige, grey, or white with a dark water line at their base. Some lean while others stand straight.

Recent findings suggest that attached by arches, the columns are so evenly spaced that to some visitors, it resembles an ancient temple. Horizontal cracks about 30cm apart add further detail to the columns. They look like they hold up the cliffs but they simply remained after the softer cliff rock started to erode.

In a recent development, the high levels of silica, sodium, and potassium in the columns make the rock conduct heat well and cool suddenly. This led to the cracks. Similar formations exist in Guatemala, Mexico, and New Mexico.

The few people who frequent Crowley Lake have long known about the columns. Only recently, social media has started to highlight them. This is due to its seclusion on the lake’s shoreline. The only ways to access them are on foot or by boat, kayak, or 4×4. The dirt road on which you turn from Highway 395 is so steep and uneven that it can bog down vehicle. Visitors tend to drive halfway, then walk.

Despite popular speculation that these columns are an example of columnar jointing, they are not. The geological process is different. With columnar jointing, the spaces are not so far apart. A study by geologists at UC Berkeley used a combination of computer models, X-ray diffraction, and electron microscope imagery to determine how they formed. It turns out that the culprit is simply…water.

“We hypothesize that the columns are a result of instabilities at the liquid water and steam interface as cold water seeped into the still-cooling Bishop Tuff,” indicates Noah Randolph-Flagg, the study’s lead scientist.

Industry observers note that the columns formed through hydrothermal convection. Photo: Shutterstock.

Essentially, rainwater seeped down into the hot ash and started to boil, producing a mineral glue called mordonite. The boiling water formed a column of steam which carried the mordonite upward through the rock. Thus, the mineral hardened the rock, leading it to remain standing while the surrounding rock eroded. This process is called hydrothermal convection or circulation.

According to Randolph-Flagg, it only took 100 years to form these columns. The study also states that “the liquid water–steam interface probably is the source of the instability that generates columnar flow.”.

As for the erosion of the cliffside, the reservoir’s water levels fluctuate throughout the year with the seasons. After the completion of the reservoir, the columns started to reveal themselves. The constant rise and fall as well as a repeating freeze-thaw cycle caused the tuff to recede. It revealed the columns and also hollowed out the cliffside to form shallow caves. Take care when going into these little caves or pushing on the columns, as they might not be as stable. As the cliff continues to erode, we should see more of these columns.

In a recent development, the arches resemble Moorish architecture. Photo: Shutterstock.

In terms of the Long Valley Caldera, scientists have closely monitored its activity, which has been increasing since the 1980s. Since it is a one of only 20 supervolcanoes in the world, they have paid close attention to its potential for eruption, despite its status as inactive.

There have been small earthquakes and signs of movement in the earth as if it were “breathing.” This is seen in Yellowstone, another supervolcano. While there are no immediate signs of an impending eruption, the caldera’s history and current activity suggest that it is possible.

#125268. Causing a Scene: North Meets South on the AT

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 32m • 📚 Deep Dive (6327 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Causing a Scene: North Meets South on the AT

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 32 min read (6327 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~32 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Even though the Franklin free hiker shuttle isn’t until late morning, all of us at the Rock Gap shelter wake up early.
  • According to recent reports, “What the hell,” I say, walking away from the woods towards the highway shoulder.
  • In a recent development, as an approaching vehicle appears, rounding the corner in the distance, I stick out my thumb and spread a calculated I-want-something-from-you smile on my face that will hopefully be perceived instead as genuine friendliness.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Even though the Franklin free hiker shuttle isn’t until late morning, all of us at the Rock Gap shelter wake up early. We only have 3.7 miles to hike, but are feeling the eagerness of Town Energy. Ahead of the pack, Show and I descend the final steps to Winding Stair Gap at little after 8:30AM. There’s nothing to do but wait, for the next couple hours. Unless….

According to recent reports, “What the hell,” I say, walking away from the woods towards the highway shoulder. “It doesn’t hurt to try. What else are we gonna do for two hours?”.

In a recent development, as an approaching vehicle appears, rounding the corner in the distance, I stick out my thumb and spread a calculated I-want-something-from-you smile on my face that will hopefully be perceived instead as genuine friendliness. The car speeds past, making no efforts to slow down. Its windy wake rustles my hair across my cheek.

According to recent reports, usually I hate hitch-hiking. The stakes of needing to get somewhere and not knowing if or when you actually will get there feel too high to my control-freak brain. But in this scenario, with the fail-proof backup strategy of the town’s shuttle coming, eventually, for certain, I’m willing to test my luck.

I drop my pack on the ground in front of me, so I don’t have to keep standing there with it on, and so cars can more easily identify me as a thru-hiker. Show walks over to join in, standing behind me so I’ll be the first person in view. The age-old trick of using the female hiker as bait.

Industry observers note that I’m not convinced this actually works. I’ve been in many a scenario where a single guy or two men have gotten rides quicker than Show and I have. And yes, I have tried various womanly wiles such as letting my hair down when it was long and standing there in a sports bra. Neither has definitively provided a quicker ride. We do it like this anyway, just in case we happen to get a driver who perceives picking up a woman as less threatening. Or believes me to be a “damsel in distress” and wants to come to my unnecessary rescue.

Ten minutes later we’re still standing there. Raising our thumbs and curling our lips every time a vehicle appears, dropping them immediately as it blows past us. I’m not discouraged, though. We’d expected to be waiting here anyway.

According to recent reports, as a promising pickup truck rushes by, and I swear, may have even sped up at seeing us, Rufio, Cous Cous, and Noah pop out of the woods at the trailhead. They walk over to join in on the hitching, the five of us standing in a line with our thumbs out. Now we really need a pickup to fit everyone.

Recent findings suggest that A few minutes later, a silver truck approaches from the opposite direction. We don’t bother to display our thumbs since it’s not heading the way we’re trying to go. To our surprise, it begins slowing down and pulls into the parking lot. Are they here…for us? That awkward moment of trying to decipher whether you should be presumptuous and start walking over towards the vehicle, or if the person is coincidentally arriving to go for a hike.

In a recent development, fortunately this driver makes it obvious by pulling up to where we’re standing and rolling his window down. A gentleman in his 60s or 70s pokes his head out and says, “When I first drove by there were only two of you. Then I turn around and there’s five! If someone’s willing to ride in the bed I can take everyone.”.

Industry observers note that we swiftly decide amongst ourselves that Cous Cous is going to take the bed. He’s the greenest of all of us and has never ridden in the back of a pickup truck before. Let’s get this kid some life experience! We load up the bed with all of our packs and Cous Cous climbs in next to them. Show, Noah, and I take the back seat. Rufio rides shotgun.

Industry observers note that as we drive past vistas of evergreen mountain views towards Franklin, the driver shares with us that God wanted him to pick us up. He further explains that he’s always on the lookout for ways to provide random acts of kindness on His Holy’s behalf. Seeing us hitching was today’s “God shot.” Hey man, whatever got you to pull over, I’m here for it.

Industry observers note that observing the driver and Rufio sitting next to each other, a devout Christian and a hippie ex-con, strikes me as humorous. An unlikely duo to be en route together. But with Rufio addressing him politely as “sir” in his slight Texan drawl, it kind of works anyhow. It’s a beautiful thing that the trail brings so many folks together who ordinarily wouldn’t have anything to do with each other.

Sources indicate that when the man drops us off in town he insists on a prayer circle before departing. We kind of owe him one so no one objects. We gather round behind the tailgate and bow our heads. He thanks God for providing an opportunity to help us and asks Him to bless our journey ahead. We close with an Amen, thank the man, and head towards the local diner for breakfast.

Recent findings suggest that the small town vibe in the Kountry Kitchen was palpable. It’s the kind of joint where the elderly townies gather at 6AM open for a cup of Joe seven days a week. They banter with the waitresses and everyone knows each other by name. The sort of place where your local-ad-decorated mug is never fully empty because a kind woman always seems to appear with a carafe at your side by the time you’re running half full. “More coffee, hon?”.

It has been revealed that we get seated at a large table towards the back, segregating us and our smell from the other patrons. A reasonable choice by the wait staff. On the wall above the table is a poster that reads “All I need is a little bit of coffee and a whole lot of Jesus.” It makes me laugh to myself because I’ve seen it before in an entirely different context.

There’s these hilarious gay husbands who have made an Instagram Reel series out of going into Homegoods stores and reading out signs such as these to each other in an exaggerated, sassy manner. You can’t help but smile at the dramatics and the way they crack each other up. This exact sign made an appearance in one of the videos, so I can’t take it seriously. Here, down south, though? These people didn’t hang that up ironically. They’re really that big on Jesus.

Sources indicate that another thing they’re apparently big on down south? Eavesdropping. I can’t remember what exactly Rufio was doing or saying, but it doesn’t really matter. He was talking loudly (likely with some cuss words thrown in), and just generally being his boisterous self. Noah, a born and raised southern boy, became visibly uncomfortable with this occurring in the restaurant. “Hey,” he noted to Rufio, “just keep it down in here, we don’t want to cause a scene. People down here love to eavesdrop and they’re definitely going to be judging us if we’re acting out.”.

“Bruh, I AM the scene!” Rufio responded unapologetically, but he turned it down a notch, as best as he personally could.

“Yo!” Show exclaimed. “Now that should be your trail name. The Scene!” We all agreed it would be funny to have both “The Show” and “The Scene,” an inevitably dynamic duo, in the group. But alas, he’d already fully embraced the name Rufio and was unwilling to change it. We did, however, occasionally refer to him as “The Scene” going forward as a sort of secondary trail name since it was so fitting to his outspoken and flamboyant nature.

Recent findings suggest that I found this interaction to be an interesting example of how different the social culture is in the southern versus northern US. Going off what I learned from Noah, it seems southerners have a tendency towards listening-in, gossiping, and generally being all up in each others’ business. At least in small towns such as this one. As a lifelong northerner, in my experience these behaviors are not non-existent, but much less common. Up north we tend to keep to ourselves more, mind our own business.

We also may have different definitions of and tolerances for “causing a scene.” Personally, if I were to go into a casual restaurant in New England and someone was being a little loud and/or swearing in public, I wouldn’t think much of it. Unless of course it was something that was continuous for a long period of time, that’s obnoxious anywhere. But I wouldn’t bat an eye at a brief raised voice or an expletive shouted out here and there. I also wouldn’t think to intentionally listen-in on a conversation happening at the next table, nor consider that others in my surroundings are purposefully trying to listen-in on mine. And even if they are, why the hell would I care? It’s just not a thing here.

If you’re from either the north or the south in the US, weigh in! Do you agree with these differences in social norms around public politeness and business-minding (or lack thereof)? Let me know your experiences in the comments!

In a recent development, I recognize that may be a jarring headline for all of my southern readers. “Forgive my northern attitude,” as Noah Kahan would say. Promise I’m not being a deliberately crass northerner for titling this section that. Believe it or not, Ballsack is actually a person I want to tell y’all about.

If you follow a lot of thru-hiking content, you likely know that in recent years there are have been a number of Calendar Year Triple Crowners out on these trails. In case that title itself isn’t self-explanatory, these are folks who attempt to hike all three Triple Crown trails in one calendar year. Some even do what’s called a “Border to Border” Calendar Year Triple Crown (B2BCYTC) by extending the AT in both directions to touch the Maine/Canadian border and the southernmost tip of the US in Key West, Florida.

In 2025, we had Peg Leg and Punisher. This year, among the B2BCYTC-ers out there was (well, still is, as far as I know, since it is November at the time of this writing) a woman by the trail name of Ballsack.

I’ve been following Ballsack on Instagram for a number of years now, ever since I discovered her account while she was posting about her first AT thru, which I believe was back circa 2021. A woman named Ballsack? Immediately I was amused and intrigued. I came for the name, but stayed for her delightfully silly personality and raw, honest content.

In a recent development, not only was she posting photos from her various thru-hikes, but sharing a lot of writing about them. Anyone who posts well-written, long-winded captions on Instagram captures my attention, and she was no exception. I noticed one thing in particular about her content creation that she was doing differently than most others in the thru-hiking community. She was posting after as opposed to during.

Ballsack has been highly unapologetic and forthcoming about this choice of hers to do so. I regularly saw posts explaining her desire to live in the moment during the hike, and then separately process her experiences in writing, in hindsight, later on. If this idea sounds familiar to my style of trail content creation, well, this is the source.

On the CDT, when I was struggling to come to terms with the fact that blogging and hiking simultaneously wasn’t working for me, I drew on Ballsack’s example. I knew instinctively that this way was the answer, but was afraid if I posted after the fact that my audience would care less about my content because it wasn’t being presented in real time. As if time would make it obsolete. Why would anyone want to read about last year’s hike when other people are on to posting about this year’s?

Witnessing someone else doing it and maintaining a decently large following on socials made me realize that it can be done. People still care. They’re willing to wait for quality content if they like it enough, regardless of a timing gap between the happening of the thing and the recording of it. Following Ballsack’s example, I was finally able to grant myself permission to do things my way instead of how I “should” be doing it. I have no regrets. The blog is better for it, the hikes have been better for it, and I’m better for it.

Huge shout out to Ballsack—if you happen to read this, although I’m sure you won’t, because you’re a little busy right now hiking 10,000 miles!!—you’ve been a huge inspiration to me and my trail writing! Thank you for normalizing hindsight content so I could feel confident doing it too.

According to recent reports, blogging my CDT hike from home. I may not be able to walk and blog at the same time figuratively, but hindsight content allows me to do it LITERALLY.

According to recent reports, while Ballsack and I follow each other and had interacted once or twice on Instagram, we’d never crossed paths in real life. Until, with no prior warning, the door to Kountry Kitchen opened and she walked in.

In a recent development, I’d of course known she was a couple months into her B2BCYTC by now. I figured there was a good chance she’d pass us at some point on the AT this year. But in my own busyness with pre-trail preparations I’d fallen off with keeping up with any updates she was posting online. The last I’d known she was still on the Florida Trail. So even if she’d finished that, she still had everything between its northern terminus and Springer to complete. It could be a bit until she caught up to us. Wow, she’s already here? She’s cruising along! I remember thinking. (As it turned out, she had skipped ahead to start the AT and would return for the mileage gap later on.).

Having finished our breakfast, I got up to pay at the register. After checking out, I turned to walk back to our table and saw Ballsack standing next to it, chatting with our gang. As I approached, I exclaimed in excitement, “Omg it’s Ballsack!” saying the word far too loud for the southernness of the space. I’m sure any eavesdropping old ladies brunching after Bible study clutched their pearls and Noah internally cringed.

Sources indicate that ballsack turned to greet me. I could see searching recognition on her face. I knew she knew she knew me but couldn’t place me. “I’m Toddler Snacks,” I let her off the hook, “we follow each other on Instagram.” She nodded as it clicked and we expressed our IRL nice to meet yous.

She asked everyone else’s trail names.

“I’m Cous Cous,” Cous Cous stated when it was his turn.

“But what’s your full name…?” I prompted, goading him playfully.

Sources indicate that “Ughhhh,” he groaned in angst, as we all giggled. “It’s Cous Cous Sunset.” He rolled his eyes, his disapproval evident in the emphasis of “sunset.” He hadn’t fully accepted the full name yet at this point.

I don’t think Ballsack knew what to make of this with no context. After a few more minutes of chatting she mentioned she had to get going to do some town chores, but would see us later at the hostel, where we were all staying that night. The rest of us got up to do the same and we parted ways.

Recent findings suggest that our first errand in downtown Franklin was stopping by Outdoor 76, a famous outdoor outfitter that caters towards AT thru-hikers. It’s a place many novice NOBOs rely on to swap out gear that hasn’t worked out after its 110 mile field test, myself included. In 2020, I remember purchasing a upcoming sleeping pad here. The one I’d started out with, and confidently elected not to take on any shakedowns beforehand, turned out to be far more uncomfortable than my theoretical imaginings of sleeping soundly on it for 2200 miles.

Sources indicate that shoes are another major gear item NOBOs buy here. Just over 100 miles in, hikers often assess their foot pain status and decide whether their pre-chosen footwear is worth giving more time or switching up. The Outdoor 76 staff seem to be particularly knowledgeable in this department. I remember witnessing my 2020 tramily member, Spreadsheet, getting the full run down from one of the employees.

The gist of his shoe spiel that doubled as a pep talk was that by nature of hiking over 2,000 miles, we classify as “elite athletes” (his words) and we ought to look at ourselves that way. He stressed both wearing the correct footwear, and perhaps even more importantly, keeping our mileage down in the beginning, to prioritize recovery and prevent overuse injuries. I recall him specifically suggesting that our daily mileage not exceed 10 miles yet, which seems like a rather low number to many thru-hikers, especially the younger generations.

Industry observers note that having the experience I do now, I agree with this. Not the ten mile limit in particular. I think that should be determined on an individual basis according to your fitness foundation going in, thru-hiking experience level, pack weight, age, and other personal factors, as necessary. But I agree with the general sentiment of starting SLOW; more so than you think you need to. You can always speed things up later on once you have trail legs. I’ve seen enough people burn themselves out in the first few hundred miles to know that slow is the way to go at the start of a thru.

This time around, in 2026, I was dialed in on my starting kit, so there wasn’t anything that I needed to replace this early on. As I browsed the store for shits and giggles, something caught my eye. Are those…dino nugs??

I looked longingly at the dino nugs pair thinking, ugh, I love these. They literally have toddler snacks on them… But I didn’t think I could justify carrying another pair of shorts in my pack. With sadness I left them behind. Show and I signed our names on the banner beneath the register and walked out of the store towards the hostel.

In a recent development, the hostel was different from what I remembered of it on my 2020 hike. It had changed ownership, names (slightly), and layout. Six years ago it was called “The Gooder Grove” and was run in the upstairs portion of the single-family house by an eccentric man by the name of Zen, who seemed nice enough but had gone down one too many rabbit holes of conspiracy theories. Now, the hostel resided in the basement of the house, was being hosted by a hospitable former thru-hiker couple named Willow and Bluebs, and had been renamed simply “The Grove.”.

Recent findings suggest that show and I had booked their private room which had a king bed, four walls, and a door—luxuries in a hostel setting. Often times as a couple it ends up being worth it to go with private rooms in hostels when available, not only for privacy but cost-effectiveness. If you divide the cost by two it usually ends up being around what a bunk costs, and occasionally even cheaper. Pro tip if you proposal to thru-hike with a romantic partner or someone you don’t mind sharing a double bed with: don’t assume two bunks are cheaper than one private room, check the prices!

It has been revealed that after dropping off our packs, gathering our laundry for the staff to wash, and taking showers, Show, Noah, and I headed back out for our resupply run at the Ingles. We wandered down the streets of Franklin in assorted loaner clothes and ended up getting a bit lost trying to figure out how to get around a widespread construction zone that the grocery store was on the other side of. Lucky for us, Bluebs spontaneously pulled up alongside us in his SUV. He informed us we were going a roundabout way and offered to drop us off at Ingles. We graciously accepted the ride.

According to recent reports, at Ingles we ran into Sauce, Bill, and Cous Cous. Once done with our shopping, all of us besides Cous Cous (who was still inside) loitered outside the store next to the “No Loitering” sign, waiting for him so we could all walk back to the hostel together. The topic of Cous Cous’ broke nineteen-year-old status came up. We were all in agreement that, as older and more financially stable adults, we wanted to help him out here and there. We’d all heard him express his money woes and concerns over whether or not he could feasibly finish the trail on a modest $1,500 budget.

“I’m going to run back in and swipe my card for his resupply,” Sauce confirmed, and walked back towards the doors.

“Good one!” I said. “Let’s get this kid to Maine!”.

It has been revealed that A few moments later, the two of them emerged together, Sauce looking triumphant and Cous Cous irritable. “I don’t like when you guys do that!” he protested futilely. We paid no mind to his disapproval. I’d already bought his breakfast that morning, which he didn’t like either. It seemed he was quite uncomfortable accepting what he perceived as handouts. From what little I knew of his history, he’d been financially independent from a young age and worked hard for everything he had.

Left to right: Bill, Sauce, and Noah.

I want to mention that I hesitantly included this last anecdote. I neither want to sing my own praises, nor present Cous Cous as merely “the kid” or a charity case. Cous Cous was an integral member of the group. Speaking for myself, I enjoyed witnessing his genuine care for others, intellect and depth (especially as a rather young person), and his growing self-confidence as a backpacker. Sure, we all liked to joke around, bust his balls, and mildly embarrass him occasionally in an older sibling way.

But the truth of the matter is, and I believe I can speak for the whole group when I say this, we liked having him around and viewed him as an equal. And thus, all of us shared the sentiment that we wanted to share our resources with him. When it’s no setback to you personally, why wouldn’t you want to help someone else out that you care about? Hopefully he’d get used to the help. Because it was going to keep happening.

Sources indicate that later, back at the hostel, we repackaged our resupplies and organized our freshly laundered belongings for the next day. It was a relaxing evening of preparation and socialization. Show even got some doggo snuggles in with Willow and Bluebs’ good boy.

I can’t remember his name – if you know, comment it down below!

We hung out with the other hikers, including Ballsack who showed up later on. I enjoyed talking shop with her about thru-hiking and discovering, as two Fresh Englanders, we both shared the same loving appreciation for the Appalachian Trail. Both of us feel a sense of protectiveness bordering on defensiveness towards it. It’s our attempt to dispel the narrative that the AT is nothing but a more miserable and/or less beautiful experience than other trails that Triple Crown hopefuls bemoan having to “get through” to get their title. This is wholly untrue in my opinion, and it’s nice to have an ally in this belief.

Recent findings suggest that she asked me what I thought of the CDT. At this point that was the one Triple Crown trail she had yet to do any of, as far as I know. I remember responding that it was beautiful but “a grind.” Which was my truth, as I experienced it. However, Show pointed out to me later on that this may have been in poor taste to say to someone who was attempting to hike over 10,000 miles in one year. Now THAT’S a freaking grind. My apologies to Ballsack if this came across as tone-deaf or discouraging. I’m still thinking about it eight months later.

In the morning Show and I got on one of the first shuttles back to Winding Stair Gap. We rode with Ballsack and a few others, I have no recollection who. Ballsack mentioned she was attempting to hike all the way to the NOC (Nantahala Outdoor Center) that day. It would be a little over 27 mile day for her, a distance we planned to cover in two full days and a nero, for perspective.

It has been revealed that we figured she’d be long gone as soon as she entered the woods ahead of us, and told her as much when we unexpectedly bumped into her one more time at a stream crossing. She explained that she likes to take it slow and steady, hiking for more hours of the day rather than a fast pace to get all the miles in. Definitely a strategy I could get behind. It’s probably smarter not to push yourself too hard when you’ve got to do this nearly every day for an entire year.

Bear scat seen just north of Winding Stair Gap. No source teddies were seen.

Sources indicate that around lunchtime Show and I reached Wayah Bald, a popular day hike vista with a stone observation tower you can ascend to take in the 360 degree views of Nantahala National Forest. On my 2020 thru-hike this viewpoint was socked-in; I recall hiding out in the tower to escape the wind and mist while eating lunch. Today, there was some cloud cover and general moodiness in the skies, but the layered mountain views were on full display. I was grateful to again (as on Blood Mountain) get to see views I missed last time. Two for two so far on the view re-dos!

On account of it being early afternoon and our bodies feeling good, Show and I decided to push past our initial plan of staying at the Wayah Shelter. I texted the Dump Truckers group chat letting Leigh, Noah, and Cous Cous know our change of aims since we’d agreed to meet up there that night. While we were at The Grove in Franklin, Leigh had stayed somewhere else with family. We’d left Noah behind a few hours ago as he was waiting at a road crossing for a friend who was coming out to hike with him for a night. Cous Cous I believe had gotten on a later shuttle that morning and hadn’t yet caught up to us.

Industry observers note that as we continued hiking to our fresh home for the night, the Cold Spring Shelter, we suddenly began to see an increasing amount of burned forest floor alongside the trail. Soon, we were in a charred wasteland, blackened leaf duff and singed rhododendrons all around us. Only the tree stumps and the smooth dirt trail had remained unaffected. What the heck?

In a recent development, burn zones aren’t an uncommon thing to see on a thru-hike out west. I’ve walked through many before on both the PCT and CDT. They are, however, much rarer to see on the AT, and east coast in general. Due to the wetter, more humid climate, there are simply less forest fires over here.

But this didn’t look like the aftermath of a rampant wildfire based on my experience. Typically wildfires leave behind massive swaths of inches-deep dusty ash mixed with chunks of charcoal, as well as blackened dead trees, some still standing and many as downed logs. Here the forest floor was too neatly charred at surface level, as though someone had walked through with a blow torch. And the trees had been too conveniently spared, all upright, appearing alive and well. A controlled burn perhaps?

Downed logs in an old wildfire burn scar in the Bob Marshall Wilderness in Montana on the CDT in 2025.

Charred trees in a Northern California burn scar on the PCT in 2023.

Industry observers note that not long later we reached a sign that confirmed my suspicions, warning hikers that the area beyond was closed for a prescribed burn on March 6th. I checked my watch, knowing we were right around that date. Shit, hopefully it’s not the 6th, I thought.

According to recent reports, “Today is…the 7th. Ok good. So they did this yesterday. Wow, good thing our schedule just so happened to put us here today. Had no idea this was even happening,” I stated to Show.

“Yeah,” he agreed, “that would have sucked if we got all the way out here and had to turn around…”.

We pressed on past the sign further into the burn zone and began to smell campfire smoke. From a ledge where there was a break in the trees we could see a large plume of ashen gray smoke coming from the woods at the bottom of the cliff. “Guess they’re working on that area down there today,” I observed.

In a recent development, further down the trail we came upon a jumble of blackened logs that was emitting small wisps of white smoke. There were no flames, but everything else we’d seen up to this point had been fully extinguished. This was, albeit minimally, still actively burning.

Uhhh, is this supposed to be smoking still?” I halted and looked back at Show.

“Well, seeing as we know it’s a prescribed burn… I’m sure it’s fine to just… leave it alone?” I reasoned.

In a recent development, had we found this smoking log just in and of itself, outside of that context, I probably would have felt more compelled to intervene in some way. I was further comforted in this choice not to a half mile or so later when we passed a couple members of a wildland fire crew. Cool, I thought, so they are still out here monitoring this situation. That’s good to know.

Industry observers note that after a solid 15.8 miles of hiking, five of those extra and unplanned, Show and I were the first to arrive at the Cold Spring Shelter. It was a smaller than average three-walled log cabin lean-to with a metal roof. We’d seen a chance of overnight rain in the forecast so we were thankful there was still shelter space. By the looks of it, I guestimated four hikers could fit comfortably, five snugly, six sardines if you were really desperate.

Recent findings suggest that we ended up with five in the shelter that night: myself, Show, Cous Cous, Noah, and his friend Matt. Leigh had texted us back that she was only going to make it to the Wayah shelter that night so luckily we didn’t have to squeeze one more. We actually ended up apologetically turning away a few people who showed up later. With all of our pads set up it turned out that even five was pushing it.

Everyone bedded down for the night, I read a book on the Kindle app on my phone, as I always do to help me fall asleep. My eyes grew heavier and it became increasingly hard to focus on the page and comprehend what was going on in the story—my cue reading time was over. I set my phone down on the shelter floor by my pillow and drifted to sleep.

Sources indicate that rustling sounds. I startle awake. Something crinkling above. My eyes dart to my pack, hanging up under the roof awning, suspended a few feet above my head. I strain to hear against the light rain plopping down on the metal roof and to see through the blackness. The rustling starts again. Yup, its coming from my pack, I confirm. Grabbing my headlamp, I shine its red light towards my pack. The bottom of my pack cover is twitching slightly. Fuck, I think, mice.

It has been revealed that I look over at Show. He’s wide awake, as I expected. “I think there’s a mouse in my pack cover,” I whisper.

“Yeah, I can hear it,” he whispers back, “One ran across my pillow earlier. I haven’t slept at all.”.

As quietly as I can manage, I slither out of the confines of my sleeping bag and shake my dangling pack. A small fluff ball drops to the shelter floor and scurries out of sight. I remove my pack cover and stuff it in the outer pocket of my pack. At least now if the mouse gets back on my pack it won’t sound like a potato chip bag crinkling anymore.

Industry observers note that I get back in my sleeping bag and try to settle down, attempting to push down the anxiety around Show having a sleepless night. He absolutely hates mice. I knew right then this might be our last shelter sleep. Prior to the trail he had wearily conceded to give the shelters a chance on my persuasion. I had compromised that if we encountered any mice complications we would from there forward strictly stick to the tent (his preference). Welp, it was a good almost two week run. Better mentally prepare myself for packing up a cold, wet tent from now on. Possibly sometimes with rain actively falling on me while doing so. Lovely….

I’m just fading into fresh sleep when I jolt awake, again. This time it isn’t a mouse, but some commotion occurring outside the shelter’s opening. Someone is setting up a tent directly in front of the shelter. It’s still lightly raining; I can see the drops illuminated in their headlamp. I look at my watch: 10:30PM.

I roll over to face Show. He’s on his stomach, head propped up on his hands, looking out the shelter at the tent-pitcher.

“Did someone just get here?” I whisper.

“No, it’s Noah,” he whispers back.

“What is he doing?” I ask, flopping onto my stomach for a better vantage point. The tent is partially erected, and Noah is continuously running out if view into the darkness of the woods, then returning and securing a stake down, repeat. Ohh-kayyy…?

“Dunno,” Show responds. “I guess he didn’t want to be in the shelter anymore. I’ve been watching this whole setup process. It’s been pretty entertaining since I still can’t sleep anyway.”.

“Sorry,” I sympathize. “We don’t have to sleep in the shelters anymore.”.

“Yeah,” Show sighs. “I think I’m done with them.”.

Sources indicate that tent finally pitched, Noah dips back into the shelter. “All good man?” Show asks him.

Sources indicate that “Yeah, it’s just too squeezy in here. I couldn’t sleep so I decided to just set up my tent. But I forgot my stakes at the hostel so I had to find sticks.”.

Ah, that explains the trips back and forth from the woods. We all bid each other another goodnight as Noah grabs his sleeping setup and trots out to his tent with it. By this point my mind is fully awake and alert. I figure the only way to shut it back down is to do the sleep routine all over again. I feel around for my phone, find it, and open the Kindle app.

After another hour or so of reading, my eyes once again grow heavy and out of focus. Show is snoring lightly next to me. All is well with the shelter dwellers. I fall asleep.

For even more content from me, follow me on Instagram and YouTube!

Recent findings suggest that hey, I’m Kelly aka Toddler Snacks! I'm a Triple Crowner with over 9,900 miles of thru-hiking experience under my hip belt on the AT (NOBO 2020 and 2026), LT (NOBO 2021), PCT (SNOBO/Flip Flop 2023), and CDT (SOBO 2025). I am a 35-year-old Latest Englander, right now living in NH. I'm proudly 4 years in recovery from alcohol addiction, neurodivergent (ADHD), and child free by choice (though I hope to someday be a fur mom). When I’m not hiking, I enjoy thrifting, reselling vintage & secondhand clothing online, crocheting, writing, and home reno projects. Follow along on my escapades and ruminations thereof by subscribing to this blog and following @kellylevensen on Instagram and YouTube.

In a recent development, keep it going. Newbies may be getting some good info from you. While this seemed to be a longer blog I enjoyed reading it as it put me in with your group imaging what it was like. That doesn’t happen that often for me.

Sources indicate that yeah its probably true about South more in your business. On the other hand mostly southern people are more friendly and not as rude as northerners. Everest Winds Force Climbers to Retreat

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (506 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that despite weather forecasts of high winds on Everest, the Russian team gamely left for the West Shoulder today.
  • “It’s calm right now, but the forecast is worrying,” leader Andrei Vasiliev wrote yesterday from a snow cave, where Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and Vasiliev had sheltered for the night at 6,400m.
  • The three climbers had fixed three pitches above them, according to Mountain Club, and were hoping for firmer terrain as they approached the West Shoulder of Everest, en route to the West Ridge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that despite weather forecasts of high winds on Everest, the Russian team gamely left for the West Shoulder today. But in the end, they couldn’t fight the gale-force winds, which eventually forced them back to their tent at the base of the mountain.

“It’s calm right now, but the forecast is worrying,” leader Andrei Vasiliev wrote yesterday from a snow cave, where Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and Vasiliev had sheltered for the night at 6,400m. Late today, they confirmed that the weather forecast of powerful winds was unfortunately right.

The three climbers had fixed three pitches above them, according to Mountain Club, and were hoping for firmer terrain as they approached the West Shoulder of Everest, en route to the West Ridge.

However, as we previously reported after consulting meteorologist Vitor Baia of Portugal, conditions were good Tuesday and Wednesday, but winds rose dramatically today.

Industry observers note that on a previous foray up Everest, one of the climbers heads for the West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

Industry observers note that “The winds are very strong,” Vasiliev reported. “It is impossible to work higher on the mountain.”.

In a recent development, vasiliev stated that his team is retreating to a tent at 5,600m. This is below the Lho La Pass, possibly on the Khumbu Glacier beside the vertical section leading to that col.

The question is whether the team will wait there for better conditions, retreat to their base in Lobuche, or call off the expedition.

Some charts still show a chance of variable winds tomorrow, before the jet stream hits the mountain with full force (see below).

Wind levels at around summit altitude on Everest this week, by meteoexploration.com.

Baia claims the winds will remain high every day until next Tuesday. From Wednesday on, the winds should be weaker.

The Russians set off on their third trip up Everest last Monday, hoping to summit via the West Ridge without oxygen or external support, and with no one else on the mountain.

On Tuesday evening, they checked in with Mountain Club from their tent at 6,000m, where they spent the night. The hard trailbreaking through fresh snow had slowed their pace, but they expected better conditions on the following day, as they started up steeper terrain toward Everest’s shoulder. They knew the snow up there was harder and compacted. They could even see their trails from the previous trip up, so no newly introduced soft snow had accumulated.

The Russian team on Everest’s West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

Yesterday, Vasiliev noted that they had climbed four pitches on old fixed ropes, plus another eight pitches of their own. The team is fixing ropes at the hardest sections, but not entirely along the route. As expected, snow conditions had improved with the more vertical terrain, but as Vasiliev pointed out, “it’s not exactly easy walking yet.”.

The Russian leader insists the route to the summit is doable. However, wind delays and a lack of time may ultimately end their attempt.
